articles.title: Vietnam Set to Sign Free Trade Pact With European Bloc This Week
articles.full_text:
Hanoi also says that a reciprocal trade deal with the United States is nearing completion and should be signed soon.
EFTA House, the headquarters of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) in Brussels, Belgium.
Vietnam is set to sign a European ‌Free Trade Association (EFTA) this week, as Hanoi closes in on a final trade agreement with the United States.
Reuters reported yesterday that the agreement with the EFTA bloc, which consists of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein, will be signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Swiss Economy Minister Guy Parmelin, who is currently on a trip to Asia.
The talks between Vietnam and the ETFA began in 2012 and have proceeded at a steady pace since. The two sides officially concluded the negotiations in July, following a ministerial meeting in Reykjavik that involved “intensive technical talks.”
At the time, the ETFA stated that the agreement covered “trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, investment, intellectual property rights, trade remedies, government procurement, trade and sustainable development, small and medium-sized enterprises, and cooperation and capacity building.” Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam amounted to $5.4 billion in 2025, up from around $561 million a decade earlier, according to the bloc.
Hovering over the planned signing ceremony is Vietnam’s recent arrest of a Norwegian national of Vietnamese descent on terrorism-related charges. Nguyen Duc Thuan, 52, was among three activists from the pro-democracy group Viet Tan whom the Vietnamese authorities said were arrested for entering the country illegally. Rights groups, as well as Viet Tan itself, say that the three men were abducted in Cambodia, although Phnom Penh said that it had no record of the men leaving the country.
According to Reuters, Norway’s Foreign Ministry said that ‌State Secretary ⁠Astrid Bergmal, who will attend the signing ceremony, “will raise the case of the detained Norwegian citizen with the Vietnamese authorities during her visit.” The Ministry added that it was treating Thuan’s case “as a high priority” and expressed hope that it “may be resolved without unnecessary delay.”
The imminent signing of the EFTA deal comes as Vietnam and the U.S. move toward the signing of their Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade.
Vietnam has sent its “final wording” for a trade agreement to the U.S. with hopes the deal can be quickly signed, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc told a business summit yesterday, according to Nikkei Asia.
Hanoi and Washington began negotiations on the trade deal in April 2025, shortly after President Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariff announcement, when Vietnam was hit with an eye-popping 46 percent tariff. The two nations signed a framework for a trade agreement in October that lowered the tariff rate by 20 percent, but despite months of negotiations, they have yet to reach a final agreement.
The negotiations have been held up by the turbidity in U.S. trade policy. Vietnam is currently the subject of a number of Section 301 investigations that the Trump administration has been using to get around the Supreme Court ruling in February that struck down the sweeping “liberation day” tariffs.
Vietnam was among 60 nations that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative threatened in June with tariffs of 10-12.5 percent due to their alleged failures to take action on forced labor. It is also the subject of separate Section 301 probes into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and intellectual property rights.
After meeting with Vietnamese President To Lam in New York last month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the two sides had made “substantial progress” and were “very close to reaching the final outcome.”
Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Union in 2020.

articles.title: What I Learned From a Year of Interviewing a Thai Sex Worker
articles.full_text:
Decades of research have identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the country’s illegal sex trade.
Illuminated signs on “Walking Street” in Pattaya, Thailand, a focus of the city’s sex industry.
When I started interviewing a Thai sex worker named Ying for my recent book, I was initially looking for something far different from what I eventually wrote. I wanted sleaze: something raw and stimulating. I had wanted to write about a harlot, someone immoral, for whom money took precedence over all. I had expected to write about their greed, their lack of morals and the hypocrisy that arose from an industry surrounding a deeply religious society.
My assumptions were both critical and ignorant. In every way, I had already decided on the book I was going to write without attempting to understand the mechanics or psychology behind them. What I have since learned is about choices, and how few meaningful ones there were for someone caught between family obligation, economic status, and religion. What I learned was about the life of a tortured soul, fighting to make the best of what she had.
Ying had spent most of her adult life selling sex for a living, starting when she was 19 years of age. Like many girls around her, she had dreamed of a better life – one that seemed impossible for someone born into poverty with little education. Ying grew up in Thailand’s mostly agrarian northeast. She arrived in Bangkok at the age of 17, and began work in a restaurant, where she faced long hours and poor earnings with no hope of advancement. Alongside this, she became involved in sex work, present in every nook and cranny of Bangkok. As Ying told me, “There was no choice. It was the only way to earn enough for myself and my family.”
Of course, Ying knew what she was doing. She wasn’t coerced or forced. But still the question remains: what else was available to her? The economics of her situation were inescapable. Ying was earning 6,000 baht per month at a restaurant in the early 2000s. At her peak in the sex industry, she was making close to 80,000 baht each month. Her mother back home in Isan sold food by the road, making less than 200 baht per day. Her father was an odd-job laborer earning even less. For a family like hers, the difference was colossal.
Decades of research into Thailand’s illegal sex industry have long identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the trade, which offers substantially superior earnings than the agricultural, domestic, or other poorly paid forms of work available to women who come from rural provinces. Those findings do not apply to every woman in the sex industry, but they help us understand how seemingly voluntary decisions may be constrained in practice.
Another thing became clearer through the interviews. Customers were not buying sex; they were buying a performance. Ying had to convince customers she was interested in them. To make each man feel desirable. To fulfill their every desire, no matter how detestable. Each customer was its own enterprise, and she had to remember their every eccentricity in order to encourage their return. As the industry moved online through the years, women had to improve their skill sets, to understand how to digitally market themselves. To master the psychology of attraction, and the manner in which to exercise it. Ying explained, “You have to make every man like you, or he won’t come back.”
What further surprised me was the power the customer held, even after he had paid and left. The digital world brought private encounters into the public sphere: a displeased customer could affect a woman’s future earnings by becoming an online critic, capable of influencing the market value of her services. The strength of a single review could make or break the personal enterprise she had set up for herself.
Beyond performance, Ying’s experience of sex work also revealed many personal boundaries were up for sale. Many men refused to use condoms; others demanded violent or depraved acts. Blowjob bars in particular distinguish themselves by the absence of condoms. This is an easy boundary to maintain when a sex worker is first starting out, fresh and attractive. But that balance shifts rapidly when they remain in the industry for too long, presenting them with a hard economic decision: refuse the money, or accept a greater health risk. For Ying, ageing and increasing competition intensified those decisions; she described how quickly such considerations become typical when rooted in the industry. The same market that had rewarded her youth gradually made it more costly for her to protect herself.
Her account also revealed the darker experiences of rape and abuse. In one disturbing revelation, she recounted how she was heavily intoxicated, unable to defend herself, while men around her used her sexually. Yet, when pressed on her emotions during that encounter, she seemed more bothered by her boyfriend’s inability or refusal to protect her, rather than the assault itself, a reaction I found difficult to grasp. What affected me was how nonchalant she was in recalling these experiences. It made me question if her career in sex work had created an unavoidable overlap, where consent and violation had become intertwined with her professional need to please every man she came across.
The money Ying earned was not always spent on herself. One of the recurring themes in our interviews was the importance of family responsibility and karma – and how both of these contributed to her decision to enter the sex industry. According to her strict religious upbringing, filial piety is a source of merit that can help to expunge past transgressions and ensure a positive reincarnation. Parents give their children a life, food, and protection. Children repay this debt by sending money home – something that is a moral and religious responsibility.
The same Buddhist moral universe that rejects any immoral behavior now expects a diametrically opposed sacrifice in the name of filial piety, a devastating contradiction I had struggled to understand.
Years later, that contradiction became painfully obvious when even cervical cancer could not keep Ying from returning to sex work. Her family had already structured their lives around her regular financial sacrifices and were reliant on her. She said, “There was no other job at my age that could pay so much.” Nobody forced her back after her hysterectomy. There was no trafficker waiting at her door, no one imposing their will upon her. She did it because she had no other option.
I started out with a plan to write a book about the colorful life of a sex worker. In the end, I was writing about a human being – one of us – trying her best, imperfectly and relentlessly, to survive. I now understand how morality can appear from a distance and how simple any choice can be when proper alternatives exist. And really, given those circumstances, would we have done anything so very different?

articles.title: As Indonesian Fires Continue, Singapore Records Highest Air Pollution Reading Since 2015
articles.full_text:
Jakarta is the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires that continue to rage in Borneo and Sumatra.
Air pollution hangs over Pasir Panjang in Singapore, Oct. 9, 2026.
Air pollution readings in some parts of Singapore yesterday spiked to their highest levels in more than a decade, as Indonesia came under increased pressure for its failure to contain the wildfires that have caused a dramatic decline in air quality across the region.
Hourly PM2.5 readings rose across all regions of Singapore yesterday afternoon, with the reading in the west of the island climbing to 288 micrograms per cubic meter. The reading, which is in the National Environmental Agency (NEA)’s “very high” range, was the highest recorded since 2015, Channel News Asia reported.
PM2.5 readings were in the “high” range in the south, east, and central regions of the country, while the reading in the north was in the “elevated” range.
With readings entering the “very high” range, the government also began the phased distribution of N95 masks to vulnerable segments of the population, and temporarily closed all outdoor and non-air-conditioned sports facilities in western Singapore.
Indonesia is currently battling the most intense wildfire season in 11 years, which has been exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season linked to a global El Niño weather pattern. The fires, which are concentrated mostly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, have created a haze that has affected much of maritime Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
The government of Timor-Leste, which borders Indonesia, said in a statement yesterday that it was suspending face-to-face learning activities for three days starting from ​October 15 “due to contamination by pollutant particles from wildfires in neighboring regions or countries.” This comes after the Malaysian government last week ordered the closure of schools across peninsular Malaysia, including in the capital Kuala Lumpur, due to the worsening haze.
In Indonesia, authorities said more than 280,000 respiratory problems have been recorded in affected regions since August 18. In the province of Central Kalimantan, the country’s ISPU air pollution index yesterday exceeded 1,200, four times higher than the “hazardous” level of 300.
While some fires naturally occur during the annual dry season, many are caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar, that are controlled by powerful Indonesian conglomerates. The country’s Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last month that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra had been deliberately set by individuals or companies, and pledged to investigate and punish those responsible.
As I noted earlier this week, the crisis has highlighted the inadequacy of regional mechanisms for combating transboundary haze. Malaysia this week announced that it would raise the issue with Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers ahead of the bloc’s summit in the Philippines next month.
For now, however, the region is reliant on the actions of the Indonesian government, which has been subject to increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires. In addition to a wave of complaints from Singaporean and Malaysian social media users, the frustration is now breaking into the political realm. Andrew Chen Kah Eng, the head of ​the Johor state branch of Malaysian Prime Minister ​Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition, ⁠said on Monday that Indonesia “must be held accountable” for its failure to contain the wildfires.
“Indonesian spokespeople need to stop being indifferent and unapologetic to all ASEAN countries affected, including its own people, by human-induced haze pollution,” he said. “Allowing toxic haze containing PM2.5 fine particles ​to pollute the air of neighboring countries is unacceptable.”
The following day, Malaysian lawmaker Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman called on Southeast Asian governments to lodge formal diplomatic protests with their Indonesian counterparts, suggesting that Malaysian and Singaporean banks cut off financing to Indonesian companies linked to land burning. “You need to treat them like an outcast in the region,” he said.
On Tuesday, Indonesian President ‌Prabowo Subianto ordered the mobilization of additional resources to combat the wildfires, which are particularly difficult to control due to the fact that many are in geographically remote areas and are burning on areas of dried peatland, where fires can smolder for weeks underground.
“This is a top priority for us. We must ​resolve it immediately,” Prabowo told a meeting with the relevant Indonesian authorities, according to a government statement.
Even if it is successful, without continuing action to control the activities of powerful agri-business interests, the region will continue to be subject to the choking externalities of Indonesia’s dysfunctional political economy.

articles.title: China’s Advance in the Bahamas
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities elsewhere in the region.
The December 2025, the U.S. National Security Strategy (NSS) committed the U.S. to resisting influence by extrahemispheric actors, including control over strategic assets and shipping corridors in the Western Hemisphere. Today, China has accumulated a strategically problematic commercial presence and web of influence relationships in the Bahamas. The archipelago is just 80 kilometers from the United States at its closest point, nearer than Cuba. U.S. military maritime routes for deploying and sustaining forces go through the islands, which the State Department has called the U.S. “third border.”
Beijing’s presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities in Cuba, the Panama Canal, the Port of Chancay, Peru, or the “Deep Space Radar” facility in Neuquen, Argentina. However, China’s influence in the Bahamas is just as problematic, both in peacetime and if the U.S. had to transit through the archipelago to deploy and sustain forces supporting action against the Chinese in the Indo-Pacific. While that presence appears more commercial and political than military, it includes a labyrinth of China-controlled businesses in the Bahamas and relationships with its political, military, and commercial figures that could give Beijing options to observe – and potentially threaten – U.S. forces.
Chinese commercial ventures in the Bahamas boost Beijing’s influence – and in the worst case could support and provide cover for People’s Liberation Army or Ministry of State Security operatives. Such ventures include port operations, hotels and resorts, other construction projects, and an array of telecommunication and electricity sector activities.
The Hong Kong-based firm Hutchison is the operator of the Bahamas’ principal port and container terminal at Freeport, as well as its cruise ship terminal. Hutchison is currently engaged in a $100 million modernization effort there, bringing cranes and other equipment that have been associated in the past with data security concerns.
China’s flagship commercial ventures in the Bahamas include the $4.2 billion Baha Mar resort, owned by Macau-based Chow Tai Fook Enterprises.  The venture’s Chinese-owned builder, China Construction America (CCA), was found by U.S. courts to have caused $845 million in damages by defrauding and breaching its contract with the original developer Sarkis Ismirlian. 
Other significant Chinese commercial operations involving CCA and its owner, the China State Construction and Engineering Company, include The Pointe, the associated Margaritaville Resort, and the nearby British Colonial Nassau hotel. The China-based owners have long defied Bahamian government control with the workers they maintain on the property. Examples include the government’s arrest of 65 Chinese nationals doing renovations on the British Colonial Hotel with improper work authorizations. The Pointe was also found to employ 229 Chinese nationals and 35 other foreign workers versus only 90 Bahamians, although the Chinese company’s agreement with the government required that 70 percent of the workers be locals. 
Beyond hotels, Chinese companies have established a presence through a loan-financed hospital, renovation work on the national stadium, which they previously built, and a gifted “demonstration farm,” creating an opening for regular visits by Chinese personnel.
In the telecommunications sector, which presents risks for the compromise of sensitive government, commercial, and personal data, Huawei is a major supplier to the national telecom operator ALIV, as well as BTC. In 2013 Huawei Marine Systems was selected to upgrade BTC’s BDSNi fiber-optic network, including submarine cables.
In the equally sensitive digital surveillance sector, China’s Hikvision provided more than 2,000 cameras at the Chinese-operated Baha Mar casino, among other work in the country.
Chinese companies also have a significant presence in the Bahamas’ energy sector, particularly solar projects. Examples include Chinese-based Sungrow, which provided an energy storage system on Sampson Cay, and Chinese-based Kehua and GSL, which similarly supplied solar sector products and services. Huawei advertises itself as an integrator for solar solutions in the country.
As a complement to its investments in the Bahamas, the Chinese has built an extensive web of relationships and influence with military, political, and other figures.
According to their own reporting, the Royal Bahamas Defense Force (RBDF) and Royal Bahamas Police Force (RBPF) regularly send personnel to China for courses. Six RBDF personnel participated in training at Chinese military, naval, and air force institutions in 2025. Specifically, RBDF personnel have attended training in China on maritime law enforcement and Chinese language.
On the police side, RBPF Deputy Commissioner Leamond Deleveaux reportedly attended a “Peaceful Resolution Course” in China.
For security forces, such personal relationships have been complemented by periodic gifts of material, including two Tiger armored vehicles in August 2017, equipment for the military band in November 2024, as well as donations of advanced workout equipment, jet skis, and harbor patrol equipment from the Chinese-affiliated Baha Mar Foundation.
The web woven by Beijing through its people-to-people diplomacy, however, extends far beyond the military. The Chinese government reportedly brought 100 Bahamians to China during the past year alone, including parliamentarians, senior security officials, doctors, nurses, students, and business representatives. In July 2026, China brought representatives from both of the country’s major political parties, the Progressive Liberal Party and Free National Movement, to Beijing for party-to-party consultations. 
During the past year, the Chinese hosted significant Bahamian groups for the first “China-Bahamas Forum on Dialogue Among Civilizations,” and separately, the first  “China-Bahamas Trade and Economic Cooperation Forum.” In October 2026, 23 Bahamian doctors and nurses are scheduled to travel to China for a medical event.
For a country with a population as small as the Bahamas, the Chinese government has been very active in courting its journalists, particularly those from The Tribune, Eyewitness News, and other organizations. Prominent recent examples include Leandra Rolle of The Tribune, who attended a July 2026 seminar in China called “on Media Co-operation on World Political Parties”; Genea Noel of Eyewitness News and Alicia Wallace, who attended a China-paid three-week Caribbean Media Exchange in June-July 2026; and Jade Russell from The Tribune, who spent three weeks in Shanghai in April 2025 for a training program for International Young Talents from “Belt and Road Countries.”  Less recently, Ricardo Wells of The Tribune went on four-week visit to China in May 2018; Rashad Rolle, also of The Tribune, attended a three-week journalism seminar in September 2015; and Eric Rose, of the Bahamas Information Services, served as a panelist in a July 2015 film festival event.
Many of these trips resulted in enthusiastic op-eds on China and the “lessons” it offers the Bahamas.
Beyond media, as in other countries, the Chinese government-staffed Confucius Institute at the University of the Bahamas has played an important role in capturing young Bahamians interested in China, its language, and culture. What began as a Confucius Classroom in 2009 became a full Confucius Institute in October 2012. By 2019, the institute had trained over 1,000 students and had brought over 100 Bahamian teachers and students to China.
While the majority of Chinese engagement in the Bahamas is not military in character, the extent of the presence and influence it affords China in a country just 80 kilometers from U.S. shores – and along routes strategically important for the U.S. in a war in the Pacific – should draw Washington’s attention. Given the U.S. administration’s strong record in acting on the policies and priorities it has highlighted in the NSS, that possibility should make the Chinese presence in the Bahamas a matter of concern for the Bahamian government as well.
The December 2025, the U.S. National Security Strategy (NSS) committed the U.S. to resisting influence by extrahemispheric actors, including control over strategic assets and shipping corridors in the Western Hemisphere. Today, China has accumulated a strategically problematic commercial presence and web of influence relationships in the Bahamas. The archipelago is just 80 kilometers from the United States at its closest point, nearer than Cuba. U.S. military maritime routes for deploying and sustaining forces go through the islands, which the State Department has called the U.S. “third border.”
Beijing’s presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities in Cuba, the Panama Canal, the Port of Chancay, Peru, or the “Deep Space Radar” facility in Neuquen, Argentina. However, China’s influence in the Bahamas is just as problematic, both in peacetime and if the U.S. had to transit through the archipelago to deploy and sustain forces supporting action against the Chinese in the Indo-Pacific. While that presence appears more commercial and political than military, it includes a labyrinth of China-controlled businesses in the Bahamas and relationships with its political, military, and commercial figures that could give Beijing options to observe – and potentially threaten – U.S. forces.
Chinese commercial ventures in the Bahamas boost Beijing’s influence – and in the worst case could support and provide cover for People’s Liberation Army or Ministry of State Security operatives. Such ventures include port operations, hotels and resorts, other construction projects, and an array of telecommunication and electricity sector activities.
The Hong Kong-based firm Hutchison is the operator of the Bahamas’ principal port and container terminal at Freeport, as well as its cruise ship terminal. Hutchison is currently engaged in a $100 million modernization effort there, bringing cranes and other equipment that have been associated in the past with data security concerns.
China’s flagship commercial ventures in the Bahamas include the $4.2 billion Baha Mar resort, owned by Macau-based Chow Tai Fook Enterprises.  The venture’s Chinese-owned builder, China Construction America (CCA), was found by U.S. courts to have caused $845 million in damages by defrauding and breaching its contract with the original developer Sarkis Ismirlian. 
Other significant Chinese commercial operations involving CCA and its owner, the China State Construction and Engineering Company, include The Pointe, the associated Margaritaville Resort, and the nearby British Colonial Nassau hotel. The China-based owners have long defied Bahamian government control with the workers they maintain on the property. Examples include the government’s arrest of 65 Chinese nationals doing renovations on the British Colonial Hotel with improper work authorizations. The Pointe was also found to employ 229 Chinese nationals and 35 other foreign workers versus only 90 Bahamians, although the Chinese company’s agreement with the government required that 70 percent of the workers be locals. 
Beyond hotels, Chinese companies have established a presence through a loan-financed hospital, renovation work on the national stadium, which they previously built, and a gifted “demonstration farm,” creating an opening for regular visits by Chinese personnel.
In the telecommunications sector, which presents risks for the compromise of sensitive government, commercial, and personal data, Huawei is a major supplier to the national telecom operator ALIV, as well as BTC. In 2013 Huawei Marine Systems was selected to upgrade BTC’s BDSNi fiber-optic network, including submarine cables.
In the equally sensitive digital surveillance sector, China’s Hikvision provided more than 2,000 cameras at the Chinese-operated Baha Mar casino, among other work in the country.
articles.summary: Beijing's presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities elsewhere in the region.

articles.title: Brewing in Japan: Price-Fixing Probes Test Consumer Confidence
articles.full_text:
The Japan Fair Trade Commission’s secretary general issued an unusual public warning against cartel-like activity amid rising prices.
The Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) is investigating suspected price-fixing in the beer and ice cream industries. While the jury is still out on the hops and frozen milk, Japanese consumer sentiment may already be at stake. How the agency handles these cases could shape consumer confidence in the economy during prolonged inflation.
On September 2, JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo began a regular press conference outlining the agency’s 2027 budget. What followed was not routine. Instead, Iwanari issued an unusual public warning against cartel-like activity amid rising prices. He said he could not recall a similar warning by the JFTC secretary general in his more than 30 years at the agency. 
The statement came as prices for more than 8,000 consumer items were expected to rise during Japan’s autumn price hikes. Rising prices reflect a range of pressures on companies, from high energy prices to domestic logistics challenges. Iwanari acknowledged that price increases were a normal part of economic activity, even if they had a “severe impact” on daily life in Japan. The JFTC is concerned, however, that companies might use rising costs to justify coordinating price increases with competitors.
Five weeks later, the JFTC began investigating the country’s four largest beer companies over suspected coordination of price increases through an industry organization between 2022 and 2025. The move followed a similar investigation launched in June into six ice cream companies over suspected price-fixing.
Like the ice cream probe, the beer investigation has drawn extensive domestic and international media coverage. A Yomiuri Shimbun editorial described the alleged conduct as a “serious betrayal of consumers.”
The investigation could reinforce the broader perception that companies are seeking greater profits during an already difficult economic period. Japanese media have already drawn a parallel between the current investigation and the JFTC’s report on beer pricing in the 1990s, which resulted in no charges. 
Japan’s experience of the 1990s also offers a useful reminder of how consumers react to economic uncertainty. In 1997, Japanese wages peaked at 4.67 million yen just as the Asian financial crisis began. These high wages did not necessarily translate into increased spending. 
The financial crisis, combined with the domestic policy misstep of raising taxes, contributed to a more defensive consumer mentality. Low- and middle-income Japanese households began to save more as a precautionary move. Consumers increasingly bought only necessities and focused on cost. Retailers cut prices in response, helping bring about “price destruction” (価格破壊). The shift disrupted traditional pricing practices and promoted a more cost-conscious way of consuming.
Today’s economic conditions differ from those of the 1990s. Still, the lessons about consumer behavior remain relevant. In August, Japan had its eighth consecutive month of real wage growth (up 1.5 percent year over year). At the same time, household consumption fell 3.1 percent, marking the ninth consecutive month of declining spending. The divergence suggests that growing purchasing power has not translated into increased spending. The figures suggest consumers may be becoming more cautious throughout 2026.
The government of Japan recognizes the challenge of maintaining consumer confidence and strengthening household purchase power. Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s proposed  reduction in the food consumption tax seeks to put more back in consumers’ pockets. Equally important is ensuring companies compete fairly and that prices are not shaped by unlawful coordination. 
The JFTC’s investigation addresses this concern and aligns with the goals of the recent Food System Act. The act seeks to promote “reasonable food prices” by basing price formation on the necessary costs of sustainable production, enabling producers to keep operating while still ensuring “stable food security” for the public.
Beer and ice cream are not the same as vegetables, but they do offer daily enjoyment for many consumers. Both investigations will test the JFTC’s ability to prevent collusion and protect fair competition. The outcomes will matter beyond the industries involved and will likely shape public confidence in how prices are set. 
The JFTC’s challenge, then, is to ensure companies compete fairly as Japan adjusts to prolonged inflation. If consumer confidence weakens, households may once again become even more defensive in their spending, as they did 30 years ago.

articles.title: The Trump-Xi Summit Exposed the Problems in China-US Crisis Management
articles.full_text:
Military communication channels become bargaining chips precisely when a crisis makes them indispensable.
U.S. President Donald Trump salutes during the playing of the U.S. national anthem at a welcome ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping (left), Sep. 23, 2026.
Xi Jinping’s September visit to Washington ended without a major breakthrough on trade or artificial intelligence safety. Most media coverage focused on the ceremony and the limited results. The official accounts, however, raised important questions about crisis management, which has gone largely undiscussed. 
China’s readout said the two militaries had “agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding as soon as possible on strengthening crisis communication and prevention.” The White House “fact sheet” did not mention that commitment. A later South China Morning Post report said a U.S. official denied that the discussion had taken place. 
Before any MoU can improve crisis management, Washington and Beijing first need a consensus that they agreed to pursue such a mechanism.
China and the United States already have several ways to communicate during military tensions. These include the Defense Telephone Link, direct contact between their leaders, and regular meetings between defense officials. They have also agreed on rules for military encounters at sea and in the air. 
Yet having these arrangements in place does not mean they will be used when a crisis occurs. Officials may delay answering a call, and political tensions might lead either government to suspend talks altogether. The proposed memorandum should therefore focus on keeping existing contacts available when they are most needed.
For more than a year after then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s August 2022 visit to Taiwan, senior U.S. and Chinese military officers had few opportunities to speak directly. Beijing had canceled talks between theater commanders and suspended other defense meetings in protest against the visit. The military contacts themselves were not the source of the disagreement, but they became part of Beijing’s response. 
Presidents Xi Jinping and Joe Biden eventually agreed to resume military talks when they met in California in November 2023, and the U.S. Department of Defense welcomed the move. But restoring contact after a leaders’ meeting is one thing; making sure those channels remain open when relations are strained is another.
The current Defense Telephone Link is not designed for situations that require an immediate response. According to the International Crisis Group, arranging a call normally involves giving 48 hours’ notice, and the other side has another 24 hours to respond to the request. Senior officials may be able to work with these rules when arranging meetings in advance. An emergency – say, an aircraft collision in the South China Sea – would leave little time for such procedures. By the time a call was arranged, commanders might already have made decisions without hearing from their counterparts. 
The 2001 EP-3 collision offers another example of how difficult communication can be during a military crisis. The U.S. embassy tried to contact Chinese officials after the collision between U.S. and Chinese military aircraft, but received few answers during the first 12 hours. Washington had little information about how Beijing was handling the incident. 
The Defense Telephone Link had not yet been established in 2001, making the circumstances different from today. But recent precedent is not encouraging either. In early 2023, after the U.S. military shot down a Chinese surveillance balloon that had overflown the U.S. mainland, the U.S. defense secretary tried to arrange a call with his Chinese counterpart. China reportedly rejected his request for contact. 
That episode underscored the limited value of existing crisis management mechanisms. When urgent calls go unanswered, military officers have to make decisions with limited information about the other side’s intentions.
The proposed crisis management MoU needs to handle these two problems. Even if regular military talks break down, both sides should still be able to reach each other in an emergency. It should also require an acknowledgment within 30 minutes of an urgent message being sent. The officer receiving the message would simply confirm that it had arrived and that the information was being checked. Neither side would have to admit fault or agree with the other’s account at this stage. They could leave those disagreements for later, once the immediate risk had been dealt with.
For Beijing, accepting a message is different from deciding how to respond to it. Chinese officers may have to consult their superiors before commenting on an incident, particularly one involving sovereignty or military activity. That process can take time. A simple reply verifying receipt would allow those discussions to continue without leaving Washington unsure whether its warning had been heard. Beijing could still decide what to say after reviewing the incident, while keeping the military line open during the most urgent stage of a crisis.
The International Crisis Group has called for crisis simulations in which Chinese and American officials examine how each side might respond as tensions develop. A hypothetical aircraft collision over the South China Sea would be a useful scenario for a joint exercise before the November Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The U.S. military could make the initial test call and wait for a response from its Chinese counterpart, following the same procedures that would apply in a real incident. The exercise would give both sides a chance to see how long a message takes to reach the officer responsible for answering it. Any delay caused by the need to seek approval would become apparent. 
An emergency channel should focus on what is happening at the time of a crisis. If an incident occurs, both sides need to know where it happened, whether anyone was injured, and whether their forces might come into contact again. They should not have to settle wider disagreements before sharing such information. Questions over Taiwan, technology restrictions, and U.S. military deployments can still be discussed through existing diplomatic and defense channels. Keeping these issues out of emergency communication would allow officers to deal with the immediate situation without waiting for progress in political negotiations.
Xi’s remarks in Washington called for the Chinese and U.S. militaries to “maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” Leader-level diplomacy can authorize this work, but that doesn’t guarantee progress. By the next Trump-Xi summit at APEC, both governments should at least confirm the same commitment and complete a test of the contact route. The MoU itself may take longer if the two sides are still negotiating its terms.
The leader-level summits will matter more if the two governments can agree on how to handle calls during a military crisis. In the past, political disputes have led Beijing to suspend military exchanges with Washington. The same problem could arise again, leaving officers unable to contact their counterparts at a critical moment. One way to prevent this would be to keep emergency hotlines separate from regular defense talks. The first measure of progress is therefore simple: whether both militaries can agree that an urgent message must be acknowledged within 30 minutes.

articles.title: For Uyghurs in Central Asia, US Diplomacy Could Be a Lifeline
articles.full_text:
By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs and resist Beijing’s coercion, Secretary Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be leading a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders to Uzbekistan this coming weekend. With this visit, Rubio has an opportunity to give hope to Uyghurs worldwide by publicly raising their plight in Central Asia. 
In 2019, then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo raised the Uyghur issue publicly at a meeting with Central Asian foreign ministers, urging them not to send Uyghurs back to China. Pompeo pressed the issue again with Kazakh leaders during a 2020 visit. His words resonated deeply, and Uyghurs in Central Asia felt like they finally had an advocate. Rubio now has an opportunity to reaffirm and strengthen that message. 
Central Asia is both a critical refuge and a dangerous crossroads for Uyghurs fleeing China’s genocide. More than 400,000 Uyghurs live in Central Asia – making up the vast majority of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan. China’s transnational repression extends deep into the region. Central Asian governments face mounting pressure from Beijing to silence Uyghur activists, suppress Uyghur civil society, and deport refugees to China.
Amid these conditions, Uyghurs in Central Asia face suffocating uncertainty. Some who escaped China’s abuses are in hiding. Many Central Asian-born Uyghurs self-censor out of fear. They are pressured not only by Beijing, but also by Central Asian governments that worry about Chinese retaliation. When we speak privately with Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, and others, we hear sympathy and support for Uyghur communities, but also fear of repercussions should they raise Uyghur human rights issues publicly. They fear not just provoking China, but angering their own governments.
As a result, Uyghurs in these countries often have no one to speak for them. In Central Asia, nearly every sizable ethnic minority group has a neighboring state that may intervene when their rights are violated – except the Uyghurs. Uyghurs have no government defending their rights, no state advocating for their safety. When Uyghur refugees escaped into Kazakhstan in the past, local Uyghurs who quietly offered food or shelter were themselves detained or threatened. This is what happens in a region where China’s shadow looms large and where silence has become a survival strategy.
Rubio has long been one of the most prominent American voices defending the Uyghur people. As a senator, he co-authored the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, groundbreaking legislation that barred goods made with forced labor from entering the U.S. market. During his secretary of state confirmation hearing, he pledged to press Thailand not to deport at-risk Uyghur refugees. However, the U.S. failed to stop Thailand from deporting 40 Uyghurs to China in February 2025. These individuals disappeared and their fates remain unknown.
This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy. With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China. International law is clear: no one should be returned to a country where they face torture, detention, or other grave abuses. The principle of non-refoulement is not optional. Uyghur refugees who are returned to China face near-certain detention and abuse.
The trip should also highlight U.S. policy to work with other governments to resist the expanding apparatus of Chinese influence. The same companies who helped build the surveillance state in the Uyghur region have exported their technology to Central Asia. Governments in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan have adopted “smart city” surveillance networks with facial recognition cameras and data-monitoring tools that enable the tracking of Uyghurs. Beijing-backed hackers have used telecommunications networks to spy on Uyghurs in Kazakhstan. Under pressure from the CCP, the Kazakhstan government sentenced 19 Kazakh activists to prison for peacefully protesting the Chinese government’s policies in East Turkistan.
With Uyghur life under assault in our homeland, especially after the implementation of China’s “ethnic unity” law, diaspora communities in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan have become vital guardians of our people’s history. They deserve the freedom to promote their culture, language, and traditions without fear.
The Uyghur people have not forgotten Rubio’s past advocacy. By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs from deportation, resist Beijing’s coercion, and safeguard the cultural and human rights of Uyghur communities, Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.
A key objective of this visit must be to show that commitment endures – and that the United States will take concrete action to counter China’s malign influence in the region.

Governments in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan have adopted “smart city” surveillance networks with facial recognition cameras and data-monitoring tools that enable the tracking of Uyghurs. Beijing-backed hackers have used telecommunications networks to spy on Uyghurs in Kazakhstan. Under pressure from the CCP, the Kazakhstan government sentenced 19 Kazakh activists to prison for peacefully protesting the Chinese government’s policies in East Turkistan.
With Uyghur life under assault in our homeland, especially after the implementation of China’s “ethnic unity” law, diaspora communities in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan have become vital guardians of our people’s history. They deserve the freedom to promote their culture, language, and traditions without fear.
The Uyghur people have not forgotten Rubio’s past advocacy. By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs from deportation, resist Beijing’s coercion, and safeguard the cultural and human rights of Uyghur communities, Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.
A key objective of this visit must be to show that commitment endures – and that the United States will take concrete action to counter China’s malign influence in the region.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be leading a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders to Uzbekistan this coming weekend. With this visit, Rubio has an opportunity to give hope to Uyghurs worldwide by publicly raising their plight in Central Asia. 
In 2019, then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo raised the Uyghur issue publicly at a meeting with Central Asian foreign ministers, urging them not to send Uyghurs back to China. Pompeo pressed the issue again with Kazakh leaders during a 2020 visit. His words resonated deeply, and Uyghurs in Central Asia felt like they finally had an advocate. Rubio now has an opportunity to reaffirm and strengthen that message. 
Omer Kanat is executive director of the Uyghur Human Rights Project.
articles.summary: By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs and resist Beijing’s coercion, Secretary Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.

articles.title: Russia’s Arrest of a Japanese Journalist Deepens the Freeze in Japan-Russia Relations
articles.full_text:
The case of Hokkaido Shimbun correspondent Imai Yuki could chill reporting from Russia’s Far East and narrow the space for even limited diplomatic engagement.
Russia’s detention of a Japanese journalist on espionage allegations has triggered a diplomatic protest from Tokyo and raised fresh concerns about press freedom, threatening to further strain relations between Japan and Russia amid the ongoing war in Ukraine and their longstanding territorial dispute.
On October 13, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had detained a correspondent for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun in the Far Eastern Sakhalin region. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Imai Yuki. Russian authorities said he was apprehended a day before his planned departure from Russia and transferred to Moscow, where a court ordered his detention until December 12. Espionage convictions in Russia can carry prison terms of up to 20 years.
The FSB alleged that Imai collected information about Russia’s defense capabilities under instructions from Japanese intelligence. Russian state media said the information allegedly concerned residents of the Russia-controlled Kuril Islands, including islands claimed by Japan, who had been mobilized or volunteered to fight in Ukraine.
The allegations have not been independently substantiated. Imai held press accreditation issued by Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and reporting on military recruitment and the human consequences of war is a legitimate journalistic activity.
Russian state television broadcast footage of masked officers handcuffing a man and his subsequent appearance in a Moscow courtroom. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was establishing the facts while prioritizing its correspondent’s safety.
Japan’s Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu said on October 14 that Japanese diplomatic missions had requested information, humanitarian consideration, and fair and impartial treatment. Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru acknowledged that Japanese officials had not yet been able to contact the detained journalist.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to protest the detention and Moscow’s unilateral announcement without prior explanation to Tokyo. Japan again requested prompt information and swift access to the detained journalist.
Zakharova, the Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, accused Japan of using accredited journalists for intelligence gathering and linked the case to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow and its defense buildup. She also claimed that this was not an isolated incident.
On October 5, just eight days before the FSB announced his detention, Imai published an article on the Hokkaido Shimbun’s website titled “A Glimpse of North Korea in Sakhalin.” He described an encounter with two North Korean men in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk and observed that North Korean workers appeared more numerous than when he arrived two years earlier. Imai also cited an acquaintance who said North Koreans were helping support major construction projects in the city.
For the Hokkaido Shimbun, Sakhalin and the disputed islands are neighboring communities with longstanding historical and economic ties to Japan. The arrest could have a chilling effect on Japanese journalism in Russia’s Far East. If reporting on military recruitment or the human costs of war risks being characterized as espionage, Japanese news organizations may reconsider assignments, while local sources may become reluctant to speak. Reduced independent reporting would make an already opaque relationship harder to understand, increasing the risk of misperceptions.
This isn’t the first time Russia has accused a Japanese journalist of espionage. In 2019, a Kyodo News correspondent was detained in Vladivostok over suspected collection of military information. However, in that case the journalist was told to leave Russia within 72 hours and departed the following day. Imai instead faces a criminal investigation and potentially years in prison. The contrast underscores the seriousness of his situation: Imai’s arrest could raise the specter of hostage diplomacy, complicating Tokyo’s efforts to secure his release.
Russia’s 2023 arrest of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich provides a troubling precedent. He received a 16-year prison sentence before being released in a multinational prisoner exchange in August 2024. Imai’s case could become entangled in broader diplomatic negotiations, although there is no evidence that Moscow detained him for that purpose.
The detention of a Japanese journalist will make any eventual diplomatic thaw between Japan and Russia more difficult. Japan imposed sanctions following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow subsequently designated Japan an “unfriendly country” and suspended peace treaty negotiations. The two countries remain divided over four Russian-administered islands that Japan claims as its Northern Territories.
Tensions intensified when President Vladimir Putin visited one of those islands – known in Russia as Iturup and as Etorofu in Japan – in August 2026. A subsequent visit by a Chinese provincial delegation drew another Japanese protest, highlighting growing coordination between Moscow and Beijing.
Security tensions now dominate Japan-Russia relations, while meaningful strategic dialogue has largely disappeared. Imai’s continued detention could make even limited efforts to restore contacts, including humanitarian visits by former island residents, more difficult.
Yet geography makes complete disengagement unrealistic. Japan retains interests in regional security, fisheries, and Russian energy supplies, including liquefied natural gas from Sakhalin.
Tokyo must therefore protect its citizen and defend press freedom while preserving the diplomatic channels necessary to secure Imai’s release.
How Moscow handles Imai’s case will test whether the two governments can maintain the basic communication needed to protect citizens and manage disputes, even while their wider relationship remains frozen.

articles.title: In Confronting China, The West Needs Partners in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward Southeast Asian countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners, and those are hard to come by.
Leaders from across Southeast Asia will be meeting in Manila on November 10 for the upcoming ASEAN summit. This is the same date on which the China-U.S. trade truce was set to expire. While the September 24 summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump has widely been characterized as “heavy on pomp and light on substance,” it did deliver one tangible benefit: more time. The extension of the trade truce offers Washington a modicum of breathing room. With that extra time, engaging leaders at the ASEAN summit should be top of the U.S. priority list. 
Meanwhile, Europe is signaling a greater willingness to confront China’s unsustainable trading practices. The limits of this relationship must be managed, so that Western countries can reindustrialize and regain market share. However, that effort should not come at the cost of compromising economic partnerships with countries in Asia. 
Since 2020, ASEAN and China have been each other’s largest trading partner. Furthermore, Southeast Asian countries have come to rely heavily on China as a provider of intermediate goods. Economic partners in Asia are restrained in their options; for them, some form of relationship with Beijing remains unavoidable. Thus, as the West seeks to shift its relationship with Beijing, it must not do so at the cost of Southeast Asian countries who are willing to cooperate toward a fairer global trade picture.
The U.S. and European position is valid. China is fully integrated into the global economy, and continues to be a manufacturing powerhouse. Problematically, however, Beijing seems to have abandoned its attempts at fixing its domestic consumption issues, as it also looks ahead to an impending demographic crisis. While the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) may outwardly project that it can sustain a globally competitive manufacturing sector, analysis of its economic outlook reflects that Beijing is far more restrained in the kind of development it can pursue. Crucially, however, China’s massive trade imbalance is likely a symptom of internal factors, and not a concerted policy objective. 
The CCP’s legitimacy continues to be derived, in large part, from its ability to guarantee domestic economic prosperity. As such, the regime’s targeted growth rates can be observed as a political goal, with overarching implications for the economy. In past years, to achieve a consistent 5 percent growth rate, Beijing has leveraged subsidies and targeted sectoral investments, while growing its exports. The net effect of these policies has resulted in a competition crisis marked by diminishing returns amongst different industries, which is further compounded by the problem of weak domestic consumption. A less ambitious growth target this year, coupled with Xi’s call for “high-quality growth,” signals that there is pressure to restructure aspects of the economy. 
Further, in the context of both global and regional trade, Beijing itself has shown an unwillingness to keep trade relationships entirely separate from its political ambitions. A study of China’s relationship with trading partners, published in 2020, has revealed a trend of politicization over time. Researchers considered the case of China-U.S. trade, and their findings were intriguing: “A positive shock to America’s exports to China leads to persistently worse relations with China… It stands to reason that Chinese officials genuinely do feel that China’s relations with the U.S. worsen when the U.S. increases its exports to China.” 
Trade activities themselves are not necessarily immune from political effect, and Chinese officials are sensitive to greater market penetration by foreign countries. In effect, this also demonstrates Beijing’s unwillingness to work toward a balanced trading relationship, and its preference for exporting more than it consumes, unless it is importing energy and commodities.
Southeast Asian countries have no choice but to confront this reality. Despite Beijing’s territorial claims in the South China Sea, China’s neighboring states continue to seek agreement on economic issues where it is possible. Interdependence runs deep, as evidenced by China’s $296 billion trade surplus with ASEAN in 2025. There is simply no other option for Southeast Asian countries seeking to move up the global value chain. 
This does not mean that these countries are unaware of Beijing’s coercion, or that they are not responding. Yet, with few international options, they are exposed to Beijing’s attempts at intertwining foreign aid with its regional ambitions. To that end, while simultaneously increasing its trade surpluses, China has also created parallel institutions such as the Belt and Road Initiative, the Silk Road Fund, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which have been used as leverage to reward countries that support its political objectives.
It is a fundamentally positive development that the West is looking to take a stronger stance against China’s global trading practices, in pursuit of a more balanced relationship. This position opens the door to Western reindustrialization and stimulates a push for innovation, while harboring high domestic political support within democracies. However, both Washington and Brussels must not lose sight of the constrained position of Southeast Asian countries, which rely on Chinese intermediate goods to develop and rise within the global value chain. A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward these same countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners; and those are hard to come by. 
For Brussels, an alternative would be its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), with the goal of stimulating market access between the West and its Southeast Asian partners. For Washington, the fact that it has become ASEAN’s largest export market is a positive step, but subsequent policies should seek to displace China as the supplier of intermediate goods without punishing Southeast Asian countries seeking to develop away from Beijing.

His research focus is strategic and security studies, with a current emphasis on China's military development. articles.title: The Uyghurs Who Fought in Syria’s Civil War
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy.  This conversation with Emily Feng – author of “Our Hearts Burned for Home: Uyghur Militants in Syria’s Civil War” (Columbia Global Reports 2026) and award-winning correspondent for NPR – is the 530th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”  
What was the impetus behind your reporting on Uyghur militants in Syria’s civil war?
For years, I had been reporting on the ground on the Xinjiang region and the sweeping detention campaign that began in early 2017. And one of the reasons cited in rare official comments from Beijing about why authorities were detaining and arresting hundreds of thousands Uyghur people mentioned the presence of Uyghur “terrorists” in Syria and Afghanistan, but offered no evidence and since these places were nearly impossible to access, no one had done interviews with any of these supposed Uyghur militants.
In late 2024, it suddenly became possible to go to Syria after the surprising collapse of the Assad regime there and the end of a terrible civil war. Coincidentally, I was in nearby Lebanon when the Assads fled to Russia, and I ended up spending much of the beginning of 2025 in Syria.
Imagine my surprise when I saw Uyghur fighters milling about Syria! Indeed, there were thousands of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and I was later to discover, their role in the civil war had been much more impactful than anyone expected.
But I sensed there was much more to the story about these Uyghur fighters than Beijing’s narrative – that these were masterminds behind fatal attacks on Chinese civilians who were now hellbent on destroying China. I wondered what had made them leave their families and livelihoods behind to live in an active war zone, and how they had transformed themselves from hairdressers and engineers and teachers into hardened militant fighters, working in alliance with Arabic-speaking, Syrian rebel groups.
I was also sensitive to the possible implications of reporting on Uyghurs. In no way is their existence in Syria justification for the detention and arrests, mostly without real due process, of so many Uyghur citizens of China. I resolved to find a way to contact the Syrian Uyghurs and interview them – a difficult task, as they had operated as a secretive and highly-disciplined force for more than a decade – and learn more about why they had come to the Middle East.
Analyze the factors propelling Uyghur militants to join the civil war and how they contributed to the overthrow of the Assad regime.
I don’t want to give too much away here! The details are in the book. But in short, many Uyghurs who ended up in Syria had initially hoped to put down roots in Turkey, where a sizeable Uyghur diaspora already exists. However, Turkey does not want these Uyghurs, and it has stymied their ability to get residence documents and even aided in their deportation back to China.
Turkey happens to share a long, mostly unfortified border with northern Syria, however, where a rebel-held swath of territory had been established in a growing civil war. And so that’s where a lot of Uyghurs headed, because Syria was not checking documents or asking for visas, frankly. All of them were also looking for a constructive way to help Uyghurs back in Xinjiang, or East Turkestan as the Uyghurs call it, and they hoped Syria would become a base to fight back politically or militarily against the Chinese Communist Party.  
A good number of Uyghurs had also already heard of the possibility of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and they were eager to train militarily. An active war, one Uyghur commander later told me, was free practice.
The Uyghurs’ wholehearted embrace of violence for the sake of establishing an independent Uyghur state is controversial, I should mention, among the Uyghur diaspora globally. But of the five dozen or so interviews I did with Uyghur fighters and their families, all of them described experiences where they felt diplomacy or political activism had failed them, and they felt they had nothing left to lose anymore by taking up arms.
The deadly race riots that began July 5, 2009 in Urumqi, which left scores of both Han Chinese and Uyghur Chinese dead, was a real turning point for many Uyghurs I met. The mob violence they witnessed from all parties that week and the ensuing crackdown and racism Uyghurs experienced in the aftermath convinced the majority of the fighters I spoke to to seek their fortunes in Turkey and later Syria.
What surprised me the most after weeks on the ground in Syria with Uyghur fighters was discovering the reach and breadth of the Uyghurs’ role in the Syrian civil war. The participated in major battles, played a key role in helping rebels with Hayat Tahrir Al-Sham (HTS) take Aleppo, and eventually marched into Damascus to establish the new government. HTS’ Ahmed Al Sharaa, now Syria’s president, privately credits the Uyghurs with being a consistently loyal, effective fighting force, and for that reason, the Uyghurs now have an unusual political purchase in the new Syria.
Explain the difference between the Turkestan Islamic Party (TIP) and East Turkmenistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and how China views their respective identities.
Both of these entities are part of a broader movement of Uyghurs who have taken up arms and seek to establish an independent Uyghur homeland in the Xinjiang region. I found evidence that members of both groups still maintain communication links, and some of the earliest TIP fighters in Syria initially tried to train with ETIM officials along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
But to call ETIM in particular an organization would be a stretch, based on what I was able to find. The ETIM-linked fighters I met said there were never many Uyghurs along the Af-Pak border, many were killed in American bombings, training was nearly impossible due to the difficult geography of the place, and there were ideological differences between the more relaxed Uyghurs and the more conservative al-Qaida-linked and Taliban fighters there.
TIP, the Syria branch of this nationalist Uyghur militant movement, was much more successful. They became highly disciplined and managed to remain organized, sharing scarce financial resources in self-sustaining communities in Idlib, in northern Syria, and setting up robust social services for a growing Uyghur population that has now reached 20,000 men, women, and children.
While TIP also maintained substantial links to al-Qaida affiliated groups, including with HTS, for years, these links later became problematic and internally divisive as TIP and HTS tried to brand themselves as politically more mainstream and welcoming to Syrians and Uyghurs of all castes. Yet TIP remains controversial within Syria, and also within much of the Uyghur diaspora community, who view their militant past with distaste.
Why are Uyghur militants controversial in Syria?
The Syria Uyghurs find themselves in an awkward position. At home, they were the oppressed. In Syria, they are widely viewed as oppressors, in the eyes of Syria’s many minority communities.
Foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, are viewed with fear and suspicion, as the civil war quickly devolved into a proxy war for various nation states and Islamist groups. Many remain in Syria in peacetime, creating resentments among Syrians who wish for the foreigners to return to their home countries. All the time, Uyghurs are confused with Uzbek fighters, and so many Syrians also do not know why the Uyghurs came to Syria in the first place, and do not understand why they cannot simply return to China.   
During the civil war, the Sunni Uyghurs were active in besieging Shiite Syrian villages. They were frequently attacked by Hezbollah proxy forces and retaliated against Shiite populations in response. And for many years, the Uyghurs occupied and lived in several Shiite and Christian villages whose residents had fled in advance of Sunni Islamist groups like TIP arriving, which sowed more distrust and fear among Syrian minority communities who are increasingly on edge under the Sunni HTS-dominated government in Damascus. The Uyghurs maintain they are friendly neighbors and open to Syrians of other faiths and have tried to moderate their religious beliefs somewhat, but there are often significant cultural and linguistic gaps between them and Syrians, which the Uyghurs themselves sometimes do not even fully grasp.
Finally, there were also reports that the Uyghurs were among the perpetrators, alongside Syrian government soldiers, of horrific massacres of mostly Alawi Syrians in 2025. I found no evidence to suggest Uyghurs were involved, and they have no interest in doing so, as involvement would certainly imperil their still uncertain and vulnerable status as stateless refugees in Syria.
Assess the role of Uyghur militants in China-Syria relations and the implications for China-U.S. relations.
In some ways, the Uyghurs are not very important to China-Syria, or broader China-Middle East, relations. Syria has made it clear that it will not let groups on its soil threaten China, even though they also have made it clear they will not send the Uyghurs to China, as Beijing has demanded.
For China however, the Uyghurs are the top issue for them in Syria, and successive diplomatic delegations to Damascus have always mentioned TIP and the Uyghurs as the dominant concern Beijing has for the new government.
The result is that Gulf states, notable Saudi Arabia, have become major investors in Syria’s post-war reconstruction. China was once one of Syria’s top economic partners before the civil war, and it does not look like it will regain that position.
It will be interesting to see how the Uyghurs navigate their future in Syria. Will they buy land and build houses — setting up a much more permanent community in Syria? Will their children born in Syria still maintain strong Uyghur identity links and a commitment to set up a Uyghur state, when they feel more and more wedded to their Syrian upbringing as the years go by?

articles.summary: Insights from Emily Feng.

articles.title: How Australia’s Gambling Lobby has Successfully Avoided Any Reform
articles.full_text:
Political donations, lobbying, and community influence help gambling companies block major policy reforms and protect huge profits.
Gambling businesses in Australia have a long history of effectively influencing and controlling government policy and regulation over a national pastime that makes Australians the world’s biggest gamblers per capita. The gambling industry can wield that level of control because it turns over AU$244.3 billion (2022–23) and generates more than AU$10 billion a year in gambling tax revenue to financially stretched state governments. This substantial financial contribution from gambling provides access to government decision-makers.
Meanwhile, gambling businesses have adopted parts of the tobacco industry’s “corporate playbook” to resist regulation. These tactics have allowed the gambling industry to effectively avoid regulation and instead allowed them to expand their highly profitable commercial activities.
Gambling businesses are well resourced because the products they sell are extremely profitable, and they have worked hard over many years to ensure gambling remains deeply embedded in Australian social life. A key development toward that came with the introduction of gambling machines, known as poker or “pokie” machines, into suburban social clubs from 1956 onward, and later into pubs and hotels. This helped make gambling seem like a normal part of community life. In most Australian states and territories (except Western Australia, which restricts poker machines to a single casino), poker machines are widespread and operate largely without question in venues that are also used for family meals and social and sporting activities. 
The development of these social clubs in New South Wales was particularly important. They helped provide sporting and recreational facilities in new postwar suburbs at a time when governments were unable to provide enough financial support for community infrastructure. This gave the clubs a strong community image and helped make their gambling activities more acceptable.
This approach continues today. It is not unique to Australia. Gambling businesses around the world use similar strategies, sometimes described as the “alibi model.” Clubs NSW, the largest gambling network in Australia, has carefully maintained this tradition and uses it whenever possible to promote the image of these social clubs as organizations that give generously to their communities. The close connection between local community clubs, sporting organizations, and some of Australia’s largest commercial gambling operators makes it harder to challenge the normalization and influence of the gambling industry.
Gambling operators are also among Australia’s biggest political donors, according to research. Political donations can provide access to decision-makers, which can then give gambling businesses greater influence over policies that affect them. Australia has also developed a strong “revolving door” between politics and the gambling industry. 
There are some restrictions on politicians taking jobs after leaving office, but the definition of a “lobbyist” is narrow. It generally excludes people working directly for companies or industry associations to influence government. As a result, many people involved in lobbying are not subject to the same rules. Former senators, premiers, ministers, political advisers, and senior public officials have taken jobs with some of Australia’s largest gambling companies, sometimes soon after leaving public office.
Hospitality is another form of influence. This can range from MPs given private boxes at major sporting events, or the sports minister attending football grand finals and tickets for MPs attending the Melbourne Cup racing carnival, to “policy briefing” lunches and dinners for the minister responsible for oversight of the gambling industry at expensive restaurants. 
These benefits may have to be declared, but the conversations that take place are not made public. The access provided by hospitality can be significant. A politician may spend several hours with an industry representative at an event, giving the host much more time and access than they would normally have during a visit to a parliamentary office.

The federal government has weaker rules around political transparency and integrity, with limited enforcement and relatively weak penalties. Once again, the gambling industry responded quickly, with wagering companies taking the lead.

The gambling industry provides a clear example of how the corporate playbook can be used to prevent reforms that could significantly reduce gambling harm. The reason is simple: the all-powerful gambling industry knows only too well that effective regulation could reduce their revenues and profits.
