articles.title: Can the China-US Detente Last?
articles.full_text:
Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
The recent thaw in China-U.S. relations – highlighted by reciprocal visits by President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping – raised the prospect of a more stable relationship between the world’s two largest powers. After years of escalating tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic mistrust, both governments appear willing to step back from the brink. The emerging language of “constructive strategic stability” suggests that Washington and Beijing may be converging on the need to manage their rivalry rather than allow it to define every aspect of their relationship.
But agreement on the need to manage competition is not the same as agreement on its terms. The two sides may have reached a shared conclusion that escalation is too costly without resolving the underlying disputes that drove them toward confrontation in the first place. If so, the current detente could prove less a turning point than a temporary adjustment in a much longer strategic contest.
The history of Soviet-U.S. detente offers a useful way to understand this possibility – not because the China-U.S. relationship is destined to follow the same trajectory, but because it highlights a central problem of great power relations: the conditions that encourage rivals to seek restraint may also make that restraint difficult to sustain.
The current thaw cannot be understood in isolation. It is the latest stage in more than a decade of intensifying strategic competition between China and the United States.
The Obama administration’s “Pivot to Asia” signaled a stronger U.S. commitment to the region as China’s power grew. Washington presented its policy as an effort to sustain regional order, while Beijing increasingly viewed U.S. initiatives through the lens of strategic containment. Yet competition remained partly bounded by the hope that economic interdependence and diplomatic engagement could prevent rivalry from overwhelming the relationship.
The first Trump administration marked a more decisive turn. The 2018 trade war transformed economic grievances into a central instrument of strategic competition. The Biden administration subsequently retained much of the competitive framework while expanding restrictions in areas such as advanced technology. Across successive administrations, Washington’s approach increasingly treated China not simply as a difficult partner but as a long-term strategic competitor.
The escalation of 2025-26 exposed the limits of this approach. Tariffs and countermeasures, particularly China’s leverage over rare earths and other critical supply chains, demonstrated that both countries possess vulnerabilities the other can exploit. But the ability to impose costs does not necessarily translate into a sustainable strategic advantage. Escalation can inflict damage on the opponent while simultaneously disrupting domestic industries, unsettling markets, and narrowing the room for diplomatic maneuver.
This gave both governments incentives to pursue a pause. Washington wants to stabilize trade, reduce supply chain exposure, and avoid a prolonged confrontation that complicates its broader economic and strategic priorities. Beijing has reasons to ease external pressure, preserve access to important markets and technologies, and secure a more predictable environment for economic development.
Their objectives for the detente, however, might not be identical. Washington may see a truce as an opportunity to rebuild leverage and reduce dependence on Chinese inputs. Beijing may see it as an opportunity to protect its economic position, limit U.S. pressure, and consolidate gains made during the confrontation. Each side can welcome stability while preparing for the possibility that competition will intensify again.
The significance of “constructive strategic stability” therefore lies less in whether it signals a fundamental reconciliation than in what the two governments understand it to mean. Does stability imply shared limits on competition, or merely a shared interest in preventing competition from becoming unmanageable? The distinction will determine whether the current thaw can endure.
The Soviet-U.S. experience is instructive in this regard. During the Cold War, detente emerged not because Washington and Moscow overcame their ideological rivalry, but because both recognized the dangers and costs of unconstrained confrontation. Arms control negotiations and diplomatic engagement could reduce the risks of escalation even while the two superpowers continued to compete for strategic advantage.
Yet detente never eliminated the underlying sources of rivalry. Disputes over regional conflicts, military competition, and divergent conceptions of international order repeatedly strained the Soviet-U.S. relationship. Changes in strategic calculations and domestic political environments also affected the willingness of leaders to sustain restraint. Detente could manage competition, but it could not make incompatible interests disappear.
The lesson for Washington and Beijing is not that their relationship will inevitably reproduce the Soviet-U.S. trajectory. Their economic interdependence, technological competition, and regional strategic dynamics differ substantially from those of the Cold War. Rather, the historical comparison directs attention to the conditions under which detente becomes self-reinforcing – or begins to unravel.
First, relative power matters. If either side believes that time is working decisively in its favor, it may view restraint as an unnecessary concession. Conversely, if leaders conclude that neither side can impose its will without incurring prohibitive costs, compromise may become more attractive. But a temporary balance of leverage can be unstable, especially when both governments are racing to reduce their dependence on the other.
Second, detente is vulnerable to miscalculation. Measures intended as defensive preparations may be interpreted as offensive moves, prompting countermeasures that gradually erode trust. Washington’s efforts to diversify critical supply chains and strengthen technological resilience may reduce its exposure to Chinese coercion. Beijing’s efforts to insulate itself from American economic pressure may serve a similar purpose. Such measures can make future crises less costly to withstand, but they can also weaken the mutual vulnerabilities that currently encourage restraint.
Third, domestic politics can narrow the space for compromise. Leaders must defend their policies against critics who regard accommodation as weakness or believe that strategic competition requires sustained pressure. Electoral cycles, economic pressures, and leadership changes can alter the political value of engagement. Even when leaders reach an informal understanding, they may struggle to preserve it if their domestic coalitions interpret restraint differently.
These dynamics suggest that detente is not simply a one-time choice between confrontation and cooperation. It is an ongoing contest over the boundaries of acceptable competition.
The central question is therefore not whether the current China-U.S. detente will last, but what would make it more resilient.
One indicator is whether diplomatic engagement produces mechanisms that can survive political shocks. Regular communication, crisis-management procedures, and clear expectations about military interactions would matter more than the symbolism of leader-level meetings alone. 
Another sign is whether both sides develop a more consistent understanding of the limits of competition. They need not agree on the ultimate distribution of power, but they must have some shared sense of which actions risk turning rivalry into a crisis.
A third indicator is how each government uses the breathing room created by detente. If restraint primarily enables both sides to prepare for a more intense confrontation, the thaw may postpone rather than resolve the next crisis. If it creates incentives to preserve communication, contain disputes, and cooperate where interests overlap, it may gradually acquire a more durable foundation.
Washington and Beijing may be learning that neither can easily defeat the other without paying an unacceptable price. But recognizing the costs of escalation is only the beginning of strategic stability. Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition. The same reduction in tensions that makes diplomacy possible can also give both sides time to reduce their vulnerabilities and reassess their strategic positions. That is the paradox of the current moment. 
The immediate thaw should therefore be welcomed without being mistaken for a permanent settlement. The ultimate significance will depend on whether the two powers use restraint to establish more predictable rules for managing rivalry – or simply to prepare for the next round of confrontation.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s First Dollar Bond Can Wait
articles.full_text:
The BNP government plans to issue sovereign bonds in December amid slow economic growth, fiscal strain, rising dollar bills, and a global downturn in the bond market.
Bangladesh is set to issue its first-ever sovereign bond denominated in dollars, most probably in December. The initiative aligns with the current Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government’s economic vision to strengthen the country’s bond and capital markets and reduce reliance on IMF and World Bank loans.
Initially, the government plans to issue bonds between $500 million and $1 billion, offering a regular yield, known as a “coupon,” of 7-8 percent to bondholders.
For months, Bangladesh has struggled to attract foreign direct investment and raise funds through the capital market, with zero initial public offerings since March 2024, while its banking sector has been distressed, with overwhelming non-performing loans. Amid the worsening economic situation, IMF loans came with stringent conditionalities to raise revenue collection and cut public spending, which at times means cutting social welfare expenses for the most underprivileged. Hence, the government’s decision to cancel the IMF loan and issue its debut sovereign bond in dollars promises autonomy in fiscal decision-making and an alternative channel to increase dollar reserves.
However, fiscal conditions, combined with the global bond market outlook and political instability, suggest that Bangladesh may not yet be ready to bear the cost of issuing the bond and making regular coupon payments in dollars.
Historically, Bangladesh has met its loan repayments while maintaining steady reserves, except during 2022-2024, when it faced a temporary balance-of-payments crisis due to the contraction in the global supply chain following the pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war. The current external balance sheet signals a positive outlook, with remittances reaching a record ceiling of $35.6 billion in 2026. The public debt-to-GDP ratio is 41 percent, lower than in most of its neighboring South Asian countries, including India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal.
For developing countries, sovereign bonds establish a clear benchmark for domestic and international lenders, reducing the cost of capital. A finance ministry, considering these factors separately, could plausibly move forward.
Yet, two questions require robust answers before issuance: whether Bangladesh can meet its obligations to foreign creditors and whether its fiscal condition can support the debt.
On the first question, the record favors Bangladesh, as it has never defaulted on its loans since independence. As of June 2026, its total outstanding external debt stands at $110.93 billion, with debt servicing at $4.49 billion, about 5 percent of total export and remittance receipts. According to the Economic Relations Division, less than three months’ worth of remittances would meet annual external obligations, even in the year with the highest repayment level. This raises the question of whether the reliance on remittance inflow as the source of funding coupon payments is prudent. A global slowdown might cause remittance flows to fluctuate. For example, in September 2026, Bangladesh saw one of its slowest remittance inflows in recent times. Interest on a $1 billion bond at 7.5 percent is roughly $75 million per year, a sum the balance of payments can absorb. However, the bond is not a one-year obligation.
Second, Bangladesh’s fiscal condition requires more nuanced consideration. According to the World Bank, GDP growth fell to 3.4 percent for FY26-27, only ahead of Afghanistan, amid rising inflation. Sluggish growth combined with price inflation can affect Bangladesh’s ability to service debt in two ways. It narrows the revenue base of the Bangladeshi taka used to buy dollars to pay bondholders’ coupons, effectively depleting foreign reserves and putting downward pressure on the taka’s value. A weaker taka raises the cost of coupons owed in dollars. The correlation between local currency value and borrowing power is significant, because when the local currency’s value drops, borrowing costs in dollars rise (known as “original sin” in economic terms) and the government, rather than creditors, bears the exchange risk.
For example, Zambia, Ghana, Ethiopia, and Sri Lanka previously launched their first sovereign bonds. All four later defaulted, as most borrowed again and spent the proceeds on projects that earned no foreign exchange. Depreciation then raised the local currency cost of every coupon.
That exchange rate exposure can be costly. Since the government must pay bondholders in dollars, every fall in taka’s value makes the debt more expensive at home. At 7-8 percent interest, the dollar bond looks cheaper than the roughly 8.5 percent the Treasury pays on ten-year taka bonds, but only if the taka loses less than 0.5-1.5 percent of its value each year. Over the past decade, it has fallen faster than that, so the cheaper-looking dollar bond could end up costing more.
Additionally, Bangladesh’s foreign loan commitments are gradually dropping, meaning fewer dollars will be on the country’s external account. In contrast, grace periods on loans used to finance Rooppur, the metro rail, and the Padma rail link are ending, and external debt servicing is expected to rise to about $5.5 billion by FY30. At home, interest has become the largest item of current spending, standing at 1,275 billion taka (approximately $10.4 billion) in the FY27 budget. In short, more dollars will go out while less comes in.
On the income side, tax revenue offers little help either, as the National Board of Revenue (NBR) fell 875 billion taka short of its FY26 target. For FY27, the revenue target requires growth of more than 45 percent in one year, a target Fitch says is unlikely to be reached. Therefore, spending is likely to exceed NBR’s revenue collection target.
Initiating more sovereign bond programs, such as Panda, Samurai, Sukuk, and diaspora bonds, and oversubscription could worsen Bangladesh’s debt situation. In Zambia, for example, the country’s initial outstanding Eurobond debt rose from $750 million to $3 billion within three years, leading to its subsequent default.
Beyond fiscal pressure, Bangladesh should also consider investor sentiment in the global bond market, which is experiencing a significant sell-off. Spiking energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and the boom in the equity market are pushing bond prices lower. As a result, central banks are being forced to offer higher yields to stabilize the market. As of October 9, the U.S. Federal Reserve – the largest bond issuer – raised interest rates to 5.34 percent on 10-year Treasury bonds, the highest since 2002, while the British 30-year bond offers 6 percent – the highest since 1998. With higher-yield bonds denominated in dollars, euros, or pounds available in comparatively stable markets, along with the boom in the artificial intelligence-led equity market, the question is: will Bangladesh’s sovereign dollar bond generate any enthusiasm among foreign investors?
Politics adds further risks. Although the February election gave the BNP a two-thirds majority, the Awami League’s non-participation and a ban on its political activities are a ticking time bomb that could increase political instability and drive away risk-averse investors. Further, Sheikh Hasina – the leader of the Awami League – has said she intends to return in December, when the bond is to be priced. Investors will factor that into their considerations.
Bangladesh’s standing as a good borrower stems from prudent debt management and timely repayment over the years. However, issuing a Eurobond could change that record, since payments would have to be made in a currency the central bank cannot produce. Slow economic growth, fiscal strain, low dollar inflows, political instability, and a downturn in the international bond market mean Bangladesh should proceed with caution. The country should not take on the risk if it is not ready to meet the long-term payment obligations to its foreign creditors.

articles.title: Democracy Is Not Silence Between Elections
articles.full_text:
A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.
Screenshot of a video of Delhi Police beating protesters with batons in New Delhi, India, June 20, 2026.
In a democracy, an election’s credibility depends not only on the votes cast by citizens, but also on their confidence in the institution responsible for conducting it. India’s Election Commission (EC), a constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the integrity of elections, is therefore expected to stand above partisan interests. Yet, allegations by opposition parties and activists that the EC has favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in elections as well as processes determining who can vote, alongside questions about electoral transparency and institutional independence, have brought this constitutional responsibility into sharp public debate.
The concern extends beyond any single election or political party. When citizens begin to question whether institutions designed to act independently are functioning impartially, the issue becomes larger than electoral competition. There is something deeply political about being made to stand outside, whether outside parliament, outside a university auditorium, outside government offices, or outside the very institutions that claim to represent you. In a democracy, the distinction between being inside and outside is never merely geographical.
India is a constitutional republic founded on popular sovereignty. The opening words of its Constitution, “We, the People of India,” establish that political authority ultimately derives from the people. Yet, we often reduce democracy to a single moment, the casting of a vote. We elect our representatives, celebrate electoral victories and expect the machinery of governance to function. But what happens between elections? What happens when citizens believe their representatives have failed them? What happens when people must stand outside the corridors of power to make themselves heard? A vote determines who governs. But a voice determines whether those who govern remain accountable.
Disagreement is natural in a plural society. The problem arises when criticism is treated as disloyalty, opposition to government policy is confused with opposition to the nation, and peaceful protest is viewed as a threat simply because it challenges authority. A government may win an election, but it cannot claim ownership of the republic.
India’s democratic history cannot be told through elections and parliamentary proceedings alone. It must also be told through the people who marched, organized, protested, and challenged the established order. The freedom struggle transformed streets, villages, and public spaces into arenas of resistance against colonial rule. Ordinary people did not wait for permission from those in power to demand freedom. Their participation was central to the making of independent India.
One of the most consequential examples of public resistance in contemporary India was the anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare and his colleagues in 2011. During Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s tenure, thousands gathered at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and then at Ramlila Maidan demanding a strong Lokpal institution to investigate corruption. The movement emerged amid major corruption controversies and growing public dissatisfaction with the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government.
The confrontation was not without controversy. Hazare was arrested in August 2011 during a hunger strike, provoking further demonstrations. Yet, the movement could not simply be dismissed. Public pressure brought institutional accountability to the center of national debate, and the UPA government enacted the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013. The movement also contributed to the wider anti-establishment sentiment preceding the 2014 change of government, although it was not the sole cause of that electoral outcome.
The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) movement stands as another powerful reminder that democracy is not secured by elections alone, but by citizens’ ability to question power. Beginning in Rajasthan, rural workers and farmers peacefully demanded access to official records on wages and development spending, exposing corruption through jan sunwais (public hearings) and a historic 40-day dharna (sit-in) at Beawar in Rajasthan in 1996. Their discipline, courage and refusal to retreat showed that a protest can transform a local grievance into a national democratic demand.
The first UPA government responded by enacting the Right to Information Act in 2005, converting a citizen’s moral claim into a legal right. This landmark law empowered ordinary Indians to inspect government records and hold public authorities accountable, proving that protest remains essential to protecting transparency, justice, and democracy itself.
The lesson is significant. A government can disagree with a movement, but it cannot expect public anger to disappear merely by containing it. The MKSS movement demonstrated how resistance can compel political institutions to confront uncomfortable questions. Democracy is strengthened when public demands find meaningful institutional responses.
The same lesson emerges from the defense of civil liberties during the Emergency of 1975-77. The suspension of fundamental freedoms and restrictions on the media demonstrated how quickly democratic institutions can be weakened when political authority becomes concentrated.
The electoral defeat of Indira Gandhi’s government in 1977 subsequently showed that citizens could use the ballot to reject authoritarian excesses. Indian democracy has endured not because dissent disappeared, but because people continued to demand their constitutional rights.
The Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19, subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions. These freedoms are not absolute, but restrictions cannot become a convenient instrument for silencing criticism. In Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020), concerning the Shaheen Bagh protest in the national capital, New Delhi, the Supreme Court addressed the limits of indefinitely occupying public ways. The democratic challenge is to protect peaceful dissent while respecting the rights of other citizens.
Recent events in India’s neighborhood offer a sobering warning. In Bangladesh in 2024, student protests over government job quotas escalated into a wider uprising against Sheikh Hasina’s government. A violent crackdown and mounting public anger preceded her resignation and departure from the country. Likewise, Nepal’s Gen Z-led protests in 2025 exposed the dangers of political alienation and declining public confidence in established leadership.
These events are not templates for India, nor should violence be romanticized. India’s political and societal culture is different. They demonstrate, however, that suppressing grievances does not necessarily extinguish them. When peaceful channels of dissent are obstructed, institutions fail to respond, and citizens lose faith in the possibility of change, a political crisis can grow beyond the control of those governing. Governments that mistake silence for consent may discover too late that public anger has merely accumulated.
Democracy is not merely an administrative arrangement; it is an inheritance secured through struggle and sacrifice. A republic needs institutions where decisions are made, but it also needs doors that remain open, and institutions willing to listen when concerns go unanswered. A vote is an act of citizenship, but so is a question put to a minister, an investigation published by an independent journalist, a student assembly, a worker’s march, or a peaceful protest outside the gates of power.
The republic belongs as much to the critic as to the supporter, and as much to the citizen standing outside as to the representative seated inside. Its strength will be measured not only by how people vote, but by whether they remain free to speak afterwards, and whether those in power are willing to listen. A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.
In a democracy, an election’s credibility depends not only on the votes cast by citizens, but also on their confidence in the institution responsible for conducting it. India’s Election Commission (EC), a constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the integrity of elections, is therefore expected to stand above partisan interests. Yet, allegations by opposition parties and activists that the EC has favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in elections as well as processes determining who can vote, alongside questions about electoral transparency and institutional independence, have brought this constitutional responsibility into sharp public debate.
The concern extends beyond any single election or political party. When citizens begin to question whether institutions designed to act independently are functioning impartially, the issue becomes larger than electoral competition. There is something deeply political about being made to stand outside, whether outside parliament, outside a university auditorium, outside government offices, or outside the very institutions that claim to represent you. In a democracy, the distinction between being inside and outside is never merely geographical.
India is a constitutional republic founded on popular sovereignty. The opening words of its Constitution, “We, the People of India,” establish that political authority ultimately derives from the people. Yet, we often reduce democracy to a single moment, the casting of a vote. We elect our representatives, celebrate electoral victories and expect the machinery of governance to function. But what happens between elections? What happens when citizens believe their representatives have failed them? What happens when people must stand outside the corridors of power to make themselves heard? A vote determines who governs. But a voice determines whether those who govern remain accountable.
Disagreement is natural in a plural society. The problem arises when criticism is treated as disloyalty, opposition to government policy is confused with opposition to the nation, and peaceful protest is viewed as a threat simply because it challenges authority. A government may win an election, but it cannot claim ownership of the republic.
India’s democratic history cannot be told through elections and parliamentary proceedings alone. It must also be told through the people who marched, organized, protested, and challenged the established order. The freedom struggle transformed streets, villages, and public spaces into arenas of resistance against colonial rule. Ordinary people did not wait for permission from those in power to demand freedom. Their participation was central to the making of independent India.
One of the most consequential examples of public resistance in contemporary India was the anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare and his colleagues in 2011. During Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s tenure, thousands gathered at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and then at Ramlila Maidan demanding a strong Lokpal institution to investigate corruption. The movement emerged amid major corruption controversies and growing public dissatisfaction with the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government.
The confrontation was not without controversy. Hazare was arrested in August 2011 during a hunger strike, provoking further demonstrations. Yet, the movement could not simply be dismissed. Public pressure brought institutional accountability to the center of national debate, and the UPA government enacted the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013. The movement also contributed to the wider anti-establishment sentiment preceding the 2014 change of government, although it was not the sole cause of that electoral outcome.

articles.title: What the Ukrainian Strikes on Yandex Tell Us About Central Asia’s Digital Infrastructure
articles.full_text:
Drone strikes on Yandex data centers near Moscow triggered service outages in Central Asia, too.
Over the last weekend, three Yandex facilities in Russia have been struck by Ukrainian drones, with Russian users subsequently reporting outages across Yandex’s services. After the third strike, on a data center east of Moscow in Vladimir, Central Asian users of Yandex’s superapp Yandex Go began reporting outages too.
Yandex is one of Russia’s largest technology companies, with a portfolio that resembles a hybrid of Google and Uber, but for the русский мир, the Russian world. Yandex Search holds an estimated 72 percent of market share in Russia while maintaining an estimated search engine market share in Kazakhstan of just under 30 percent. It is with its superapp, Yandex Go – which combines ride-sharing with food delivery and other services – that Yandex dominates in Central Asia.
In 2017 Uber effectively ceded Central Asia to Yandex, agreeing to merge operations in Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus and Kazakhstan, where the two companies had previously competed. Yandex Go expanded to Kyrgyzstan in 2017 and to Uzbekistan in 2018. A 2023 effort to enter the Tajik market was defeated by Dushanbe. In 2023, Yandex bought Uber out of the joint venture, becoming the undisputed ride-sharing and food delivery leader in the Central Asian region.
On October 11, following the strike on Yandex’s Vladimir facility, Yandex customers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan began reporting trouble booking rides, ordering food and accessing their accounts. The press services of Yandex Qazaqstan, Yandex Kyrgyzstan, and Yandex Uzbekistan all acknowledged technical issues to local media outlets and said they had teams working to restore services. 
Although services have reportedly resumed, at least in Kazakhstan, Russian media reports stated that it could take months to restore operations at the affected data centers. And that doesn’t factor in possible future strikes.
Kazakhstan’s Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition reportedly issued a warning to inDrive, an alternative ride-sharing app which operates in the country, after its prices spiked during the Yandex outage. As users shifted from the inoperable Yandex Go app to inDrive, prices went up dramatically. The agency claimed that in some cases the cost of rides tripled. 
According to RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service, InDrive founder Arsen Tomsky “attributed the price hike to a sharp increase in demand and a shortage of available vehicles.”
This is just another way in which the Russian war in Ukraine has had knock-on effects in Central Asia. While complicating deliveries of KFC, plov or lagman late at night may not rank as the most critical of issues, this incident does underscore that Central Asia’s digital infrastructure remains closely linked with Russia’s. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development stressed that the personal data of Kazakh users of Yandex is safe because it is stored on servers in Kazakhstan. But the overarching architecture – the technical bits that connect a person to a driver – is not, and therefore risks posed to Russia’s digital infrastructure will continue to spill over into Central Asia. 
Ukraine, for its part, positioned its attacks on Russian data centers as retaliation for Russia’s strikes against Ukrainian data centers. Kyiv also claimed that its attacks targeted centers that provide revenue streams to Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12 that “everyone noticed” a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. The reality of that claim is, as these things tend to be, far more complicated.

articles.title: Drones and Missiles Are Rewriting the Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula
articles.full_text:
North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons is outpacing South Korea’s capacity to destroy them.
In this photo provided by North Korean state media, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attends tests of “various kinds of reconnaissance and suicide drones” developed and produced by research institutes and enterprises under the Unmanned Aerial Technology Alliance, Mar. 18, 2025.
The two Koreas have been close observers of the wars in Ukraine and Iran – not least because aspects of the conflicts mirror how both sides think they will win a potential war on the peninsula. The ongoing exchange of long-range drones and missiles, in particular, resembles the type of war both Koreas envision for themselves: a deep strike contest. To this end, both have recently begun developing low-cost, long-range attack drones, with some systems slated to be operational in the near term. 
Long-range artillery, ballistic missiles, and nuclear weapons have, so far, shaped each side’s view of the military balance and whether deterrence holds on the peninsula. Armed drones will soon enter the picture.
These drones will exacerbate the South Korean military’s existing gaps in surveilling the North. Pyongyang’s growing missile and nuclear arsenal and diversified launch platforms have made the problem acute. With cheap attack drones, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ offensive firepower will further outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy it. 
This trend is at odds with the Lee administration’s ambitious timeline for gaining wartime operational control from the United States. South Korean forces will need additional capabilities to meet the qualitative conditions previously established by the two allies.
Long-range drones – unarmed aerial vehicles with operational range far beyond the forward edge of battle along the armistice line – have been a feature of the inter-Korean military competition for the past two decades. The first known operational use was in 2010 when a North Korean reconnaissance drone was spotted during the Yonpyeong Island shelling. Since then, periodic drone incursions have been a feature of the inter-Korean low-intensity skirmishes. 
In 2014, South Korea recovered the wreckage of three North Korean drones less than 50 miles from the border. In December 2022, five North Korean drones overflew Seoul, including the presidential office, and returned North. In response, then-President Yoon Suk-yeol floated the idea of South Korean forces conducting reciprocal drone incursions into North Korea. North Korea claimed South Korean drones overflew Pyongyang in October 2024. While officially denied, public analysis of North Korean-released images visually matched developmental South Korean reconnaissance systems.
Rudimentary platforms – small, fixed-wing, turboprop, and unarmed – have featured in these largely symbolic aerial incursions so far, alongside unpowered balloons. There is no evidence that either side has employed armed drones in cross-border operations. Drones that had been operationally used on the peninsula, however, represent only a small subset of a broader inventory that includes systems with greater range and capability.
North Korea has been importing Chinese and Soviet drones and has been developing indigenous models for reconnaissance missions since the 1980s. In 2023, North Korea unveiled a high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) reconnaissance drone and a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) multi-role drone. Both are qualitatively different from its existing unmanned aircraft – the latter, for example, is capable of firing a missile – though limited numbers are in the inventory. 
For South Korea, abortive development efforts in the late Cold War resumed in the 1990s with a focus on the tactical surveillance drones supporting the Army’s ground operations. Interest in long-range systems came in the late 2000s when the Agency for Defense Development (ADD) started developing a domestic MALE, KUS-FS, and the Republic of Korea Air Force procured Global Hawks from the United States. Four Global Hawks were delivered by 2020, and the KUS-FS is expected to enter service in 2027.
The wars in Ukraine and Iran have catalyzed the two Koreas’ interest in massed, cheap, and armed long-range drones while they continue to invest in large, sophisticated unmanned systems. In 2024, Kim Jong Un ordered officials to “establish a mass-production system and begin full-scale operation” of “suicide attack drones.” Thousands of North Korean laborers, and possibly engineers, have also reportedly been sent to the Yelabuga factory in Russia producing copies of Iran’s Shahed one-way attack (OWA) drone. 
For South Korea, the ADD is developing the KUS-LM – dubbed the “K-LUCAS” with reported range and payload figures comparable to the American OWA drone called LUCAS – with plans to deploy it before 2030. The system has started trials on land and sea.
These investments by both Koreas in long-range unmanned systems, for both strike and surveillance, will alter the terms of the inter-Korean military competition. In the past few decades, the main domain of the inter-Korean military competition has become a deep strike-centric contest. The ability to wage a strategic air campaign – one not directly connected to the ground fight – is now central to how each side assesses the balance. Both sides appear to believe loitering munitions fit into this air power paradigm.
North Korea has pursued missile and nuclear weapons technology to hold at risk its neighbor and its ally, the United States, with long-range fires. South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense assessed that, in a contingency, North Korea plans a surprise massive firepower attack to create favorable conditions and force a rapid end to the war. Even absent an offensive intent, the threat of catastrophic damage from nuclear missiles and conventional munitions that bypass defenses creates a powerful deterrent intended to prevent attack and ensure regime survival. 
Under Kim Jong Un’s rule, North Korea has expanded its missile force to deliver both conventional and nuclear warheads deep into South Korea and, increasingly, beyond the peninsula. The nuclear arsenal, too, has increased both numerically and in centrality to North Korea’s security policy. The KPA Ground Force also operates thousands of artillery pieces – with sufficient range to reach Seoul – out of hardened sites concentrated south of the Pyongyang-Wonsan line.
North Korea appears to see drones as a complementary element of its deep strike strategy, enabled by mass, concealment, and dispersal. Indeed, Kim Jong Un noted three attributes that make OWA drones a needed investment for the Korean People’s Army: low production cost, simple manufacturing process, and ease of integration into existing firepower. Drone salvos launched in conjunction with ballistic and cruise missiles could overwhelm South Korea’s air and missile defenses. Their relatively low cost also reduces the economic burden of procurement on North Korea’s constrained economy. 
In response to a nuclear-armed adversary and fear of abandonment from its ally, South Korea has pursued a counterforce “Three Axis system” to serve as a non-nuclear deterrent. This idea has seen iterative conceptual updates over the past decade. Today, the approach rests on a three-pronged framework that combines preemptive strikes on North Korean nuclear and missile facilities (“Kill Chain”), multi-layered missile defense (Air Force-operated “Korea Air and Missile Defense” against ballistic missiles and the Army’s in-development “Low-Altitude Missile Defense” against artillery and short-range rockets), and overwhelming retaliatory firepower against military and leadership targets (“Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation”).
Efforts in the past five years have sought to integrate drones into the strategy. The Yoon administration established the Drone Operations Command in September 2023 with an explicit mission to develop an offensive concept of operations – before that, South Korea’s military had only used drones for reconnaissance and surveillance. Despite initial criticism of the command as redundant, and its subsequent disestablishment for its implication in Yoon’s 2024 self-coup attempt, the South Korean defense community appears to acknowledge the need for this function. The mission continues in the Defense Drone headquarters, the recently formed successor body that focuses on force development, manning, and equipping – albeit shedding any operational role to the services.
Deterrence on the peninsula holds today as both sides possess long-range strike assets that impose what, for now, are unacceptable risks and costs if the shooting starts. While ground forces remain important in both Koreas’ force structures, the main arena of the inter-Korean competition today lies in deep strike. The drone incursions in the past decade and a half introduced an additional low-intensity element to this competition. The development and eventual deployment of armed drones will create new requirements for South Korea to operationalize its Three Axis strategy and for the United States to defend its treaty ally.
South Korea’s limited intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capacity stands out as a glaring vulnerability in anticipating this future. All three “axes” of its strategy depend on a near-perfect and near-persistent intelligence picture over North Korea, to monitor leadership movements, locate concealed facilities, track mobile missile launchers and submarines, identify incoming missiles – and now, detect drone launch sites and their launches. This is a tall order. South Korea’s ISR capabilities have long been identified as a weakness, as it historically has relied on U.S. capabilities. 
ISR drones and additional ISR satellites are intended to supplement existing gaps to operationalize the Three Axis strategy, but even with systems expected to come online in the next five years, mobile targets will remain difficult to find, fix, and track. South Korea’s space-based ISR layer, in development since 2023, leaves roughly 2-hour windows between observation opportunities over potential launch sites. The South Korean Army’s Low Altitude Missile Defense, expected to come online in 2029, was designed to counter artillery threats and may be constrained by insufficient interceptors and sensor networks against drone salvos. 
Thus, in the near to medium term, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons will outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy them. In fact, North Korea’s rapid operationalization of OWA drones may require greater dedication of U.S. ISR assets to the peninsula.
The added challenge to South Korea’s defense strategy thus poses questions about the Lee administration’s ambitious push for wartime operational control transfer by the end of his term in 2030. The proposed change to the command structure of U.S. and South Korean forces has been tied to improvements in South Korea’s capabilities to lead the Combined Forces Command, including the capacity to operate its own ISR assets to meet operational requirements. The Lee administration has insisted on “no additional conditions” being placed on the transfer requirements. Yet, the deteriorating military balance in this domain will necessitate additional capability to meet the established qualitative conditions for making major changes to the Combined Force.
The author appreciates feedback from colleagues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies – Pat Bazylczyk, Mark Cancian, Emma Gargiulo, and Andy Lim – and the 2026 cohort of the National Committee on American Foreign Policy Korea fellowship.

articles.title: Pakistan Is Treating Every Grievance as Terrorism, and It’s Failing
articles.full_text:
From KP to Balochistan and beyond, instead of addressing the underlying causes of unrest, the country’s rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition.
Pakistan faces mounting political, economic, and security crises. But instead of addressing the underlying causes, the country’s rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition and treating it as the problem.
I have seen this approach firsthand in Balochistan, Pakistan’s militancy-ridden southwestern province. For years, the state has responded to political dissent and social, economic, and political grievances primarily through a security lens, via arrests, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings. The consequences have been severe: such policies have pushed thousands of youths toward a violent insurgency. But this approach is no longer confined to Balochistan.
Recent developments in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa suggest that the same logic is increasingly being applied elsewhere. On October 11, Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government led by Sohail Afridi, an ally of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Pakistani media reports said Afridi had been arrested and his whereabouts remain untraceable. 
Enforced disappearances are a longstanding practice in Pakistan, particularly in its peripheries. But the disappearance of a politician who was the chief minister until Sunday morning raises disturbing questions about the rule of law and the fate of ordinary citizens with far less visibility or political influence.
The scenes from Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s provincial capital, tell a similar story. Security forces have filled roads with brightly colored shipping containers to prevent Khan supporters from reaching Islamabad. On October 4, Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), took to the streets to demand his release. The federal government has defended the barricades and its latest actions as necessary to prevent unrest.
Such restrictions on political dissent go beyond the PTI.
In Balochistan, the authorities have confronted the Baloch Yakjehti Committee, a large grassroots movement against enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. Its popular crowd-puller leader, Mahrang Baloch, was sentenced to life imprisonment on June 22 by an anti-terrorism court, alongside fellow activist Sibghatullah, over the alleged killing of a paramilitary soldier during a protest in Pakistan’s new emerging port city Gwadar in July 2024. The court found they had incited the crowd. Baloch’s lawyers boycotted the proceedings, held inside Hudda jail, and called it a faceless trial.
In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement, another civil rights movement demanding rights for ethnic Pashtuns, has faced an intensive crackdown. Its soft-spoken, 34-year-old charismatic leader, Manzoor Pashteen, has been among those targeted, as the government has attempted to ban the movement and its leadership.
Authorities have used similar tools in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, long described by Pakistani leaders as the country’s “jugular vein.” On June 5, the Azad Jammu and Kashmir government designated the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots coalition that has organized protests over economic and political demands, as a proscribed organization under the region’s anti-terrorism law.
These are different movements, with different demands. But the state responds in a common way: it treats every political grievance as a security threat.
Laws such as the Fourth Schedule, once intended for terrorism, are also being used against lawyers, journalists, and political opponents. In particular, the controversial cyber law, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), is frequently used against activists and journalists. 
In January, an Islamabad court handed prominent human rights lawyers Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, prison terms totaling 17 years over social media posts the state called anti-state. The sentences were to run concurrently, so they were to serve 10 years. In September, the Supreme Court suspended the sentences and ordered their release on bail. Within hours, authorities rearrested them in an earlier protest case.
Since the controversial 2024 elections, Pakistan’s Parliament, the judiciary, and the media have come under intense pressure. Citizens on the periphery, especially ethnic minorities such as Baloch, Pashtuns, and Kashmiris, have little reason left to take a political complaint to those institutions.
Meanwhile, the security crisis has worsened.
The Global Terrorism Index ranked Pakistan the country most affected by terrorism in 2025. It recorded 1,139 deaths and 1,045 terrorist incidents, with Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa bearing the brunt.
An Islamabad-based think tank, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICS), documented 606 deaths and 232 injuries from militant attacks and counter-militancy operations in July 2026 alone, the deadliest month of the year to date. Most of the dead were militants: 401, against 112 security personnel and 74 civilians. The raw numbers still argue against the idea that more force is closing the war.
Some years ago, Pakistan spent millions of dollars on fencing its roughly 1,600-mile border with Afghanistan to contain cross-border attacks from militants allegedly based in Afghanistan. But militancy continues. Islamabad has since taken the war across the border. 
On March 16, a Pakistani airstrike hit the Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital in Kabul, a drug-rehabilitation center on the site of a former NATO base. Pakistan said it had struck a militant storage site. The U.N. mission in Afghanistan confirmed at least 269 civilian deaths and 122 injured. Amnesty International later said the strike should be investigated as a possible war crime.
Cross-border strikes have continued. On October 1, Pakistan launched airstrikes in Kunar and Helmand provinces in Afghanistan. The Taliban government said at least nine civilians, mostly children, were killed and 11 injured. The U.N. mission said at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine were injured. Pakistan said the strikes targeted militant hideouts and claimed 22 militants were killed.
There is a clear contradiction here. Pakistan’s leaders want to be seen internationally as peacemakers and mediators. At home, they have refused to engage politically with Imran Khan, Mahrang Baloch, the Kashmir committee, and Manzoor Pashteen, and they have preferred force with Afghanistan as well. The economic cost of that instability is why Islamabad is asking Washington for a $10 billion exchange-stabilization facility to strengthen its foreign-exchange reserves.
Western governments should be careful not to confuse that request, or Pakistan’s field Marshal General Asim Munir’s usefulness in mediating with Iran, with a diplomatic settlement. Pakistan matters to the West because of its size, its nuclear weapons, its position between South and Central Asia, and its role in regional security. Engagement with the army should not mean ignoring a provincial capital closed off with containers, civil rights movement leaders tried under anti-terror laws, or a strike on a Kabul hospital. Nor should Pakistan’s leaders assume that economic assistance or geopolitical usefulness can substitute for public trust.
Militancy cannot be excused, and the state has a legitimate responsibility to protect its citizens. But military action alone, whether inside or outside Pakistan, is not resolving the political alienation underneath the violence. Pakistan’s leaders need to face the hard questions. Why are educated Baloch in Balochistan being drawn toward a deadly insurgency? Why has resentment among Pashtun youth against the state increased? Why have large crowds in Kashmir repeatedly taken to the streets? 
The West has tried to build a relationship solely through military generals before. It did not produce a stable partner. It is unlikely to do so while the same generals answer political protest with emergencies, repress dissent with terror and cybersecurity laws, target Afghanistan with airstrikes, and then ask the West to finance the country for economic stability.
Pakistan faces mounting political, economic, and security crises. But instead of addressing the underlying causes, the country’s rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition and treating it as the problem.
I have seen this approach firsthand in Balochistan, Pakistan’s militancy-ridden southwestern province. For years, the state has responded to political dissent and social, economic, and political grievances primarily through a security lens, via arrests, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings. The consequences have been severe: such policies have pushed thousands of youths toward a violent insurgency. But this approach is no longer confined to Balochistan.
Recent developments in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa suggest that the same logic is increasingly being applied elsewhere. On October 11, Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government led by Sohail Afridi, an ally of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Pakistani media reports said Afridi had been arrested and his whereabouts remain untraceable. 
Enforced disappearances are a longstanding practice in Pakistan, particularly in its peripheries. But the disappearance of a politician who was the chief minister until Sunday morning raises disturbing questions about the rule of law and the fate of ordinary citizens with far less visibility or political influence.
The scenes from Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s provincial capital, tell a similar story. Security forces have filled roads with brightly colored shipping containers to prevent Khan supporters from reaching Islamabad. On October 4, Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), took to the streets to demand his release. The federal government has defended the barricades and its latest actions as necessary to prevent unrest.
Such restrictions on political dissent go beyond the PTI.
articles.summary: From KP to Balochistan and beyond, instead of addressing the underlying causes of unrest, the country's rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition.

articles.title: US Economic Diplomacy With Allies Becomes an Election Showcase for Trump
articles.full_text:
Investment pledges by Japan and South Korea make tempting achievements for Trump to hold up ahead of the voting.
U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan (blue tie) speaks while standing next to U.S. President Donald Trump during an event announcing new investment for the Alaska LNG pipeline, Sep. 30, 2026.
On September 28, Trump invited Iowa Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican running for an open Senate seat, to the Oval Office to announce a new $15 billion steel plant in her home state, which is being built by the local subsidiary of an Indian conglomerate. Two days later, with Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan standing beside him, Trump announced roughly $54 billion in prospective South Korean investment in the Alaska LNG pipeline. 
Notably, both announcements came a little over a month before the midterm elections. The Associated Press noted that it was “the second time in three days” Trump had paired a major investment announcement with a Republican Senate candidate in a race that had become unexpectedly competitive.
Seoul described the Alaska announcement quite differently. South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said it went “far beyond what was agreed,” while his ministry said it had not decided whether to invest or how much. The U.S. Commerce Department’s fact sheet was more conditional: the two sides had agreed to begin work on Alaska LNG, subject to commercial reasonableness and domestic legal requirements. 
Similarly, Washington also presented a roughly $22 billion Texas project and a nuclear framework valued at up to $120 billion. Again, Seoul has indicated a more cautious approach to those investments, with individual reactor projects still under review. In other words, the headline figures may not all materialize. 
The election wasn’t the driving force behind these projects or negotiations, which have been in the works for nearly a year. But the announcements have clear electoral value. On September 30, Trump said he had done “a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing.” The Iowa and Alaska events show how investment announcements involving U.S. partners are being caught up in Trump’s pre-election economic messaging. 
The approaching elections – and polling suggesting that a number of Republican seats in Congress are at risk – increases the political value of presenting long-term allied investment plans as immediate economic wins. Both South Korea and Japan had agreed to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in the United States as part of overall economic deals reached in 2025 with the Trump administration. The upcoming election may be impacting the announcement of specific projects under those investment pledges – although it’s hard to establish the connection definitively. It’s also possible that Japan and South Korea could use Trump’s sense of urgency over specific projects to leverage better terms. 
The structure of the deals is responsible for some of the confusion. The Korean and Japanese “agreements” are actually administrative arrangements that create no legally binding obligations. Under the standard timetable, actual funding is not required until at least 45 business days after an ally is notified that the president has selected a project. South Korea’s domestic law adds another layer: investments are, in principle, reviewed for commercial reasonableness and other considerations, examined by a government committee, and reported to relevant National Assembly committees before Seoul consults Washington. In other words, there’s a month-plus gap between any political announcement and the point at which money actually changes hands.
Before the Alaska announcement, Washington was pressing for faster progress, while Seoul emphasized commercial rationality. The planned announcement had already been postponed while such differences remained unresolved. The election may have given Seoul temporary bargaining room, even as Washington remained the much stronger party. When one side values speed more than the other, delay itself can become bargaining leverage.
Japan offers an important comparison because its investments have been moving more quickly. On February 17, Trump announced the first $36 billion of Japan’s $550 billion investment pledge. Tokyo’s first financing agreement came about 10 weeks later, on May 1, and provided roughly $2.2 billion for that initial batch of projects. By September, Japan had announced two project rounds totaling about $109 billion. 
The gap between announcement and financing is relatively baked in. In that sense, the midterms may be amplifying an existing practice rather than creating a new one.
When evaluating major investment announcements, it’s important to look beyond the topline figure to other data points: what the partner government has actually approved, when funding will actually arrive, and which political or diplomatic events might be impacting the timing. 
A new Japanese investment package before November 3 would strengthen the case that the U.S. election calendar is influencing announcement timing. If the next investment announcement isn’t made until the November 18-19 APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, however, it would mean the diplomatic calendar is more influential. These explanations are not mutually exclusive: an announcement can advance negotiations abroad while producing political value at home. 
The same logic applies to allied behavior. Resistance, delay, or demands for safeguards by Japan and South Korea may suggest the allies have greater bargaining room, but would not by themselves prove that electoral pressure caused a concession from the Trump administration. Remember, these investment pledges are around a year old; the process has been moving slowly from the start.
The midterms are not overhauling U.S. economic policy toward Seoul and Tokyo, but they could make the Trump administration keen to announce progress early – even before funding actually comes through.

articles.title: What the US PERM Freeze Really Costs India’s IT Industry
articles.full_text:
The immediate impact of Washington’s decision on green card certification for eight IT employers may be limited, but the freeze adds uncertainty to an immigration system already strained by decades-long queues.
On October 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor decided to stop processing PERM labor-certification requests from eight technology firms, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini. The Department of Labor said it would neither accept new applications nor process pending applications involving the named companies. 
PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the initial step in the employment-based green card process for most immigrants applying under the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. In order to proceed to the next stage, employers are required to prove that they have tried to hire Americans for the jobs in question. 
The processing of the applications has been suspended in accordance with 20 CFR § 656.31(b), which allows for the temporary interruption of services if there are grounds to believe that fraud or willful misrepresentation is involved.  
Vice President J.D. Vance accused companies that employ people on H-1B visas of creating a caste of foreign indentured servants. Notwithstanding the administration’s justification, allegations must not be confused with provided proof of fraudulent activity. 
On the heels of the H-1B controversy came reports of investigations into the J-1 visa program, involving dozens of American universities. In the context of Vance’s comments on H-1B visas and intensified scrutiny of J-1, the latest development suggest that the debate over the United States’ immigration policy and the prospects of its labor market will continue to gain momentum. This would, in the meantime, systematically erode India’s IT service sector’s integrative loop with American companies and vice versa.  
The H-1B-to-green-card process has three basic stages: entering the United States, living there as a worker, and eventually receiving permanent residency. Each of these possesses its own restrictions. 
Indian nationals comprise a significant part of successful H-1B applicants. A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ FY2024 H-1B characteristics report said that Indians comprised 71 percent of successful applicants in 2024. 
The H-1B has become an IT program. Infotech workers made up 32 percent of H-1B holders in fiscal year 2003 and averaged over 65 percent across the last five fiscal years. H-1B status permits temporary employment, subject to immigration rules and the conditions of the petition. Workers may continue working lawfully while their green card applications are delayed, provided their existing authorization remains valid. 
PERM falls under the third step, which concerns the transition from being a temporary resident to receiving permanent residency. The suspension interrupts a stage of the process for affected applications, potentially delaying workers’ transition to permanent residency. Its consequences depend on the status of each application. 
Given a massive backlog, the PERM suspension impacts individual workers. But its immediate relevance for corporate profits is limited.  
The Cato Institute estimated the U.S. employment-based waiting list to contain approximately 1.8 million people in 2023, around 1.1 million of whom are Indians. This puts the portion of Indians in the queue at around 68 percent. The report estimated the time necessary to clear the backlog for Indian applicants to be up to 134 years, with approximately 424,000 Indians expected to die before obtaining a visa.  
This might have more of an impact than it seems. Permanent residency is a significant factor in the worker’s life, affecting their decision-making and planning. Another obstacle in their employment-based residency application might disrupt their lives severely. 
Even before the PERM suspension, the U.S. immigration system was becoming more expensive and unpredictable. The Trump administration announced a $100,000 H-1B fine announced in September 2025. That was later clarified by USCIS to be applicable only to petitions made after September 21, 2025, as a one-time payment rather than an annual renewal. 
Employers are adjusting their strategies accordingly. An RBI survey tracked an erosion in on-site revenues, from $19 billion to $18.4 billion. These are wages paid to staff members who work at client facilities overseas. The reduction implies that the traditional approach of sending numerous Indian professionals to work overseas is being de-emphasized relative to other approaches to technology services delivery. 
Nasscom data revealed that Indian IT revenue totaled $315 billion in FY2025-26, up 6.1 percent, with exports of $246 billion, up 5.6 percent. The industry employed some 5.95 million workers and created about 135,000 net jobs in the past fiscal year. An American client can continue to buy software development, consulting, maintenance, and other tech services from an Indian team without requiring those professionals to be based inside the United States.  
A restriction on permanent residency might well impose genuine costs on workers while having limited impact on the revenue-generating capabilities of their employers. The impact will vary from company to company, project to project, and staffing model to staffing model, but the market’s response to the policy change need not reflect the impact on individual workers’ circumstances. 
For Indian IT companies, the PERM freeze may prove a small financial blow rather than a major threat to their business model. Most of their American revenue streams do not rely on having every employee on their payroll based in the U.S., and the fall in on-site earnings suggests an industry growing more capable of providing services beyond borders. 
For Indian professionals, the implications are more personal. A green card process that already takes years to complete has just become even more unpredictable for those considering applying, and for whose employers are affected. Even if their American jobs are unaffected, their plans for permanent residency may be set back. 
For India, the long-term impact is harder to assess. Restrictions on immigration may motivate multinational companies to invest more in local infrastructure, creating jobs and cementing India’s role as a center for tech production. But it would also shift work away from Indian outsourcing firms and toward the captive centers of their American clients. 
The short-term financial pain may be minimal. The anxiety for those affected, however, is far greater. And the longer-term challenge will be whether the U.S. can prevent a rush to move work to where it will have value, by closing access to where it currently does. 
This moment also marks a troubling low-threshold point in India-U.S. relations, almost causing an irreparable harm to the long diplomatic relationship between the two countries. First, tariffs on Indian imports, and now restrictions on skilled human capital mobility from India to U.S. companies could erode and dismantle core areas of economic integration between the two countries, which were cementing a strong political bond as well. 
Where this leaves India and its economic integration strategy viz-a-viz the U.S. (amidst a more conflicted relationship with China) should trouble policymakers more than it seems to do in the current scenario.

articles.title: Tajikistan, Turkmenistan to Import Indian Surface-to-Air Missile Systems
articles.full_text:
Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that Tajikistan and Turkmenistan are newer customers for the indigenous Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile system.
India’s growing defense industry has set sights on Central Asia for new customers. In early October, Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, speaking to Asian News International (ANI) held up the indigenously designed and produced Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile (SAM) system as a “success story.” He highlighted exports of the system to Armenia, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.
“The first customer was Armenia, which has taken multiple batteries,” Singh said. “Thereafter, we’ve also exported it to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. Production has stabilised. We have additional orders for our own services, and I’m sure there will be many more from various parts of the world…”
Singh’s comments confirmed a report from July, published in Indian business magazine BW Businessworld, which cited official data as listing Tajikistan and Turkmenistan as export destinations for the Akash system.
Although ANI reported that both India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) and the Ministry of Defense had confirmed that “Tajikistan and Turkmenistan have joined the buyer list,” neither of the Central Asian countries has commented publicly on the reports.
Central Asia’s militaries have been diversifying suppliers, but the bulk of region forces remain Soviet and/or Russian in design and procurement, with newer additions of Chinese, Turkish, Indian, and Western equipment.
RFE/RL’s Zamira Eshanova recently explained the variety on display:
Recent military parades show just how much Central Asian armies are diversifying their equipment. At its Independence Day parade in Ashgabat on September 27, Turkmenistan displayed a newly acquired Chinese FK-2000 air-defense system, adding to its existing arsenal of Chinese-made missile systems. Also on parade were a Brazilian-made A-29 Super Tucano attack aircraft and Italian-made Leonardo M-346 training jets.
Tajikistan, meanwhile, has displayed China’s HQ-17AE air-defense system, along with Chinese-made armored vehicles used to transport and protect troops. During its 2026 Independence Day celebrations, Uzbekistan also showcased Chinese J-10CE fighter jets. And, in recent years, Kyrgyzstan has acquired several types of Turkish military drones.
Essentially nothing is known publicly about the Indian defense exports to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan: the number of systems, the delivery timelines, or the prices.
More is known about the Armenia exports, which may provide some insight for Central Asia watchers. Armenia signed a $720 million deal with Bharat Dynamics Limited in 2022 for an unknown number of Akash SAMs and 15 Ashwin ballistic missile interceptors. Although deliveries were pushed back, in November 2024 Yerevan took delivery of its first Akash battery, which included four launchers a Rajendra radar. A second delivery reportedly took place in July 2025.
As the Oxus Society noted in an October 2024 report on Tajikistan’s military, “India’s military involvement in Tajikistan dates back to the early 1990s and early 2000s, beginning with the refurbishment of Tajikistan’s Ayni Airbase.” But after the base was refurbished, Tajikistan pivoted back to Russia, walking back plans for India to station its own military assets at the site. Instead, Dushnabe signed and agreement with Moscow to allow Russian forces to use the base. India has had access to, though not a permanent presence, at the Farkhor Airbase near the Afghan border.
Prior to the apparent Akash deals, India hadn’t sold any defense equipment to Tajikistan or Turkmenistan. 
The export of one type of system, if and when they arrive into Central Asian hands, won’t fundamentally alter the military supplier balance in the region. But it underscores that regional governments are looking for additional partners and pathways out of strict dependence on Russia for defense materials. Such a move introduces new problems, specially regarding interoperability – the ability of different systems to work together effectively.
